170239: A girl shut the door on seven beggars. Then one of the beggars said: "You will be possessed by the devil." A while later the girl was indeed dragged up and down the stairs by the devil. When enough had been prayed for the girl, she was freed from the devil.
170260: A mother had a child of fourteen or fifteen with extremely thin legs and a big head. Because the child had 'de oude man' (the old man, a wasting illness blamed on witchcraft), they went to the friars of Bornem. The friar listened to the people's story and then said: "In what form would you like to see her appear? If you see her appear in water, she will drown. If you see her in fire, she will burn." The mother said: "Let her appear in water." The parents were placed before a kind of theatre stage and saw the woman they suspected appear. At that moment the child could no longer be held and screamed like a cat. The witch came off the stage and fell into the water. Then the friar said: "She has not drowned yet, they will still drag for her. You must make sure she can no longer get into your house. Haven't you noticed anything?" The mother said she always saw a mewing cat appear at the bedroom window, and the friar answered: "That may be her, because they can change into anything." The mother was further advised to put a red-hot poker under the gap of the front door, because witches turned into a pekduivel (pitch devil) and could then get under the door. The mother had to have her wedding ring blessed by the friar so that she could put it under the front door. She had to lay a rosary in front of the bedroom door and burn a blessed candle in the room where the child lay. The mother followed the friar's advice. That evening there was a knock. When the mother asked who it was, a voice answered: "Your Sooike," to which the mother said: "That can't be, because she is in bed." The parents had been in bed only an hour when they heard their child screaming like a cat. They went to look and saw a cat scratching at the window of the child's room. But the cat could no longer get in.
170317: Witches made the dogs howl at night when someone was dying. They also made young people waste away and die. They could turn someone's hair grey in a single night. They could change into horses' heads and chase people in the dark in the evening.
170323: At the end of the First World War a book was found in 'Der Hoeve', where Germans had been billeted. The farmer's son read that book and so learned to work magic. When some people were on their way to the fair, the boy fixed them to the spot so they could go no further.
170341: In a house, cats kept crawling in through the drain hole for the water. A certain neighbour knew exactly what the occupants of that house were up to. After all, she appeared there in the shape of a cat. One day that woman had a broken arm.
170373: On the Latoenenhoeve the people had much misfortune. On top of that they were laughed at by their neighbours. In reality these people were being bewitched by the neighbours' daughter. A while later the neighbours laughed no more, for they themselves had become victims of their daughter's hauntings.
170375: On a farm one morning the horse had been pulled through a small hole. The cows in the stable all had their right leg stuck.
170377: A farmhand worked on a farm in Loenhout. That farmhand could make mice without tails. When the farmer told the parish priest, the clergyman came to the farm to take away the boy's magic power.
170383: On a farm where the cowshed was bewitched, the farmer kept watch at night. Around one o'clock the shed doors flew open there. After that the evil hand was gone.
170397: A man who was going to the eight o'clock Mass in Rumst met a witch on the way, who said: "You won't get there anyway." The man answered: "We'll see about that." Then the man lost his way. At midnight he ended up at the church in Waarloos.
170407: In Ekeren there used to be a farmstead called 'the Spookhoeve' (the Ghost Farm). The people often had visits from poor travelling gypsies who went about with wheelbarrows and came to ask for a place to spend the night. Among those people were also witches. When their host or hostess got up at six in the morning, his or her barn burned down. When the witch moved on to the Hof van Delft, fire broke out there too.
170410: A man saw a stalkaars (will-o'-the-wisp) by a toll barrier. It was the soul of someone who had lived near B.
170422: In the Grijshengstenhoek the devils flew about at night in a glowing cart. Wherever the devils passed, the doors and windows of the houses flew open.
170468: A bewitched woman had much misfortune in her house and fell ill. The woman went to the friars, but they could no longer save her, so she had to die. The woman's children were bewitched too, as were the cows in the cowshed. On that farm one could tear down stone bridges by hand.
170484: In Elsum there was a house that was haunted. In the evening everything there began to rattle. When the occupants went to look, there was nothing strange to be seen. Still, they left the house. As long as the house stood empty, nothing happened, but when new occupants moved in, the haunting started again. Those people also left the house, and from then on it stood empty until it was demolished.
170501: A farmer had much misfortune with his animals and his vegetables. Within one month a horse died, the chicory harvest failed and the farmer fell ill. The farmer was advised to have the brown friars read prayers over him. He followed that advice and had no more misfortune afterwards. A friar had said that near the farm lived a woman who consorted with the devil and wanted to harm him. After that, however, the man would have no more misfortune.
170511: A newly married couple rented a cart from a distant relative for half a franc a day. The owner of the cart let the couple off the debt and said: "I'll come and have coffee with you some time". When the owner did so, the farmer's wife showed her the barn and the cowshed with everything in them. Since that visit the cart owner's daughter always came to have coffee with the farmer's wife. At the same time the girl was also at home. She could be in two places at once. When the farmer's wife fell ill, she went to the abbey of Tongerlo, where she was given something she had to take for nine days. After that the witch no longer came to visit her.
170561: Whenever a woman was followed by a cat, she always believed the cat was a witch. When the woman could not churn butter, she went to the fathers of Tongerlo.
170572: A miller was always tormented by a pack of cats. One day the miller chopped a paw off one of the cats. Afterwards he found his wife in bed. She had lost a leg.
170580: In a house where banging was always heard in the evening, the little child often began to cry, saying: "A person, a person!" After a few days the people went to the friars of Lier, who advised them to ask what the ghost wanted. The ghost turned out to be the spirit of a dead relative, who came to ask for a pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel. The woman of the house then said angrily: "You never did anything for us, and now you come asking us that!" After a pilgrimage had been made for the dead person, the knocking was heard no more.
170586: A man coming back one evening from visiting friends on the Hei could not get home. He kept walking in circles because he was bewitched.
170620: A mother who lived in the Jodenstraat believed her two children were bewitched because their health was visibly deteriorating. One day the woman was visited by two gentlemen dressed in black. The woman told her story and was advised to go to the friars. The gentlemen would also go on a pilgrimage themselves. When the parents came to the house, they only got inside after laying a holy object under the threshold to drive out the devil. The friars said prayers until they were drenched in sweat. Meanwhile the chairs there danced round and round. At night the mother and father had to go walking with their children. When they did, they could not get past the café on the cattle market. One day the mother met the sorceress and gave her a sound beating. Afterwards the mother had to go to the police. The mother, however, stood her ground and wanted the police to search the sorceress's house. If the police found no books there, the woman would have to go to prison for three months. But the police soon found the books of magic.
170621: When Tist S. arrived at his friend's, he was deathly pale with fright. "Yes," Tist explained, "there was a foal in the street that flew past me!" The next Sunday the two men kept watch to catch the foal. But the animal could not be caught.
170640: A man coming back from the fair in the evening suddenly saw a large black dog standing in the road in front of him. The man was startled and cried: "If you are of God, step aside. If you are of the devil, speak." The dog moved aside and let the man pass.
170685: A woman went to the station because she needed a small lamp. On her way back the woman met a witch and dropped the lamp. To protect themselves against witchcraft, people often went to fetch holy objects, but that did not always help.
170732: A miller was annoyed by a cat that crept into his bed and scratched his arms and legs. One day the miller chopped a paw off that cat. The next day he found that his wife had lost a hand.
170734: A woman from Stabroek lay on the floor beside her bed and could not move. When the doctor was visiting a woman from the village, that woman said: "You must go to X, for she needs help!" The doctor went to the woman who had fallen, but could not make a diagnosis. The woman prayed paternosters every night, but it did not help. At night someone always came into her room. A bird had been painted on a chair, and it could no longer be removed. The sorceress could get in through the keyhole and the cracks in the door. The sorceress cut the armchairs and the coats to pieces. Coal and bacon were also stolen from the woman. When the priest brought the woman a host, the host fell to the floor.
170737: In Lichtaart a man met a cat that kept jumping in front of his feet. With a blessed stick the man struck the cat hard on the back. The animal ran off howling. The next day a neighbour lay half paralysed in her bed. She never recovered.
170742: In Waver there was a child that was bewitched. Someone always came and sat on the child's feet. One day, when the mother was stirring the porridge by the fire, she saw a cat come in. That was the sorceress who had bewitched her child. The mother said to the animal: "Come, kitty, warm your bottom", to which the cat said: "Poor kitty, warm your bottom, poor kitty, warm it now, X told me that I should warm my bottom".
170770: In Valkenswaard lived an ugly old woman who was suspected of being a witch. Some Flemings walking past the witch's orchard said to the woman's husband: "Don't you have any cherries?" The man said: "If you pay ten cents, you can pick as many as you like." The Flemings quickly climbed into the trees, but the Dutch said: "Hey, you won't get out of that tree again, you know." The Flemings had some cherries left over and wanted to give them to some children. Their mother heard this and said: "No, no, these children get no cherries here. Get out of here or the whole house will be bewitched!"
170782: For four days in a row a cat came and sat in the doorway of a house. The cat did not come in. The man grew angry and took his gun. The cat saw this and ran off between two fields. The man did not manage to hit the cat. When the man went outside the next day, that cat leapt at his neck.
170816: Some boys riding to the college saw a white rabbit sitting in the same spot every day. One day they caught the animal in a sack and took it with them. When they opened the sack on arriving home, there was a white cobblestone in it. The boys went to the priest, who advised them to put the stone back where they had taken it from. The boys went with the sack to that place. They opened the sack and saw a white rabbit jump out of it.
170818: Washing left out to bleach had to be brought in before sunset, or else the witches would come to it and the children would be bewitched. Some people who had forgotten this had a child who fell ill. After the friars had read prayers over the child, it recovered.
170826: When someone made the sign of the cross behind the back of the witch Rozeke, she turned around. A woman who had borrowed Rozeke's waffle iron could not bake a single waffle with it. When she had been given a waffle iron by someone else, the baking did work.
170839: A woman from Tongerlo who was coming back from work late in the evening was jumped on by a calf on a small bridge. The calf was in reality a werewolf that made itself carried. The woman died of the incident.
170843: On a farm a full bucket of milk was milked every evening. The milk was carried seven metres further to the well, where the jugs stood to pour the milk into. By the time that distance was covered, the fresh milk had turned into a foul, lumpy liquid. Even the pigs would not take that milk. That misfortune was caused by a witch.
170847: A farm in Heffen was haunted. At night the people there always had to get up. The doors would bang open and shut and there was noise and rumbling everywhere.
170869: A woman went to the friars of Bornem for a friendly family that had been struck by the black hand. On the way the woman saw a large dog lying on the ground, baring its teeth. In Bornem the woman was given holy water and a medal. There they asked whether it was all meant for the people or for the animals in the cowshed. One could give the friars a fee, but it was not required.
170875: A witch lived in Veerle. A girl who had been given a sweet by that witch rose up into the air in her bed at night. The girl claimed she could see the witch on the wardrobe, but the others saw nothing. The doctor was fetched and said the girl had meningitis. The girl's father then cycled to the abbey of Tongerlo. On the way he had a flat tyre twice. On top of that, the chain came off his bicycle as well. Only after two hours on the road did the man reach the friars, to whom he could tell his story. Then the man rode home in half an hour. When he got back home, his little daughter was cured.
170881: On a haunted farm in Noorderwijk all the cupboards fell over.
170917: In Varendonk there was a farm where the cows all died. People blamed the calamity on witchcraft and had a man keep watch at the farm.
170923: A man from Ranst always saw will-o'-the-wisps flying through the undergrowth along the road at night. Such lights were the souls of unbaptised children.
170932: A mother went to Lier with her little daughter. On the way an old woman jumped out, pulled the mother by the arm and said: "You'd let your daughter walk under a cart". Yet there was no cart to be seen anywhere. After that the mother fell ill. At night she always heard her again and then cried: "She's there again!", but her husband did not believe it. The woman had weighed sixty kilos at first, but grew thin until she weighed only thirty-six. One Saturday, on a relative's advice, her husband went to Dendermonde. At the very moment he was there, his wife cried at home: "Now I am cured!" The woman lived to be seventy. The friars had advised the people to do penance.
170953: A woman claimed that a black cat always walked along with her, saying: "Venneke, I'm coming with you."
170959: A farmer whose cow could not calve sent for Charel S. Charel saw that a woman was standing by the cow and said: "In God's name, keep your hands off that beast!" The next moment the calf was born.
170978: A man coming back from Nijlen one night in the moonlight saw two spotted dogs with glowing eyes in the undergrowth. The dogs did the man no harm.
170998: Every day a witch took a child out of its cradle and then covered it up again. People went to the friars of Bornem for the child. On the way to Bornem the situation improved.
171008: Will-o'-the-wisps were the little souls of unbaptised children. After someone had beckoned to a will-o'-the-wisp, the light pressed a red hand onto the door.
171010: One day a black cat came into a house through the drain hole for the water. The farmer stabbed at the cat with his dung fork. The next day a woman suspected of being a witch went about with a bandage around her head.
171056: In Retie lived a man who could work magic. One day when that man came into a house, the woman there was sewing. She dropped her thimble. She picked the thimble up and saw mice crawling out of it.
171070: A man who had stolen a horse was being chased. At a brook the man said: "They won't get across here", and so it was.
171091: A farmer found his barn full of rats. A witch had caused it. When the friars came to pray there, the rats suddenly left. Friars could only drive rats away by sending them to a richer farmer.
171092: In the Lange Beeldekensstraat there used to be two haunted houses side by side. In those houses knocking was heard and objects were seen moving by themselves. On Sundays people went there to watch the haunting.
171098: Will-o'-the-wisps were the little souls of unbaptised children wandering the earth. If you said: "I baptise you", the little soul came closer. As soon as you had made the sign of the cross, the little soul was saved. But you had to say: "I baptise you alone", or else countless will-o'-the-wisps came flying.
171112: In a bewitched cowshed the cows stood all jumbled up at night. A neighbour woman caused these strange happenings.
171120: A man riding home drunk at night met a witch, who took his bicycle from him. The next day the man saw his bicycle standing by his house again. The man was afraid of the witch, who wore a white nightgown. The witch was married and had two children.
171124: Two friends who went fishing at night between the Rupel and the Scheldt saw a dark figure walking along the dike towards them. One of the boys called out to the apparition: "You must have done something wrong in the past!" The ghost answered: "That's not true at all, that must have been you!" Then the boy remembered that some time ago he had seen a corpse with golden boots floating on the water. He had swum to the corpse and pulled off the golden boots. The ghost of that dead man was now coming back for his boots. At the place where all this had happened, the ghost jumped into the reeds and was seen no more.
171129: When people went out late in the evening, a black cat always followed them. That was a witch, who stood in the street all day long.
171165: A witch was obliged to use her power. A witch from Mechelen preferred to do harm to herself or to animals rather than to other people. Sometimes that witch set her house ablaze. It also happened that cows disappeared at the market and came back the next day. The witch also often changed herself into a frog. When hay was being brought in from a meadow, a frog crawled onto the hay wagon. The farmhand put out one of the animal's eyes. Since that incident the witch had only one eye.
171176: A mother went with her child to a friar, who said: "You will meet the guilty one on the way". On her way home the mother did indeed meet the witch. At that moment the child died.
171194: A man who had gone fishing with his brother went home alone. At the 'mennegat' (1) the man saw a large black growling dog standing in front of his wheelbarrow. The man grabbed a stick and dropped his wheelbarrow as he did so. The next moment the dog had vanished. When he got home the man took his gun and went looking for the dog. But in vain, for the animal was nowhere to be seen.
171259: It was said that J. came to haunt by the crooked oak where he had dropped dead. People only dared pass that spot with a lantern. If they had a lantern with them, the ghost came towards them (?).
171284: A witch always gave something to the children of the owner of the house she rented. Because of this those children were always ill. The children's mother went to the priest, who at first denied that witchcraft existed. Later, however, he did intervene. The people moved house. When they arrived at their new house, the witch was already standing there by the well. The priest was indeed able to help those people.
171323: A woman always came to visit a certain house. When the child's godfather was home and the woman was visiting, she always said to the child: "Pull godfather by his legs, pinch him, stick him with a pin!" The child did all this to the doll. But the godfather fell ill. After that the woman was never let in again.
171340: A man from Olen had sold his soul to the devil in exchange for a new barn that had to be finished by the time the cock crowed. He needed the barn to store his harvest in. When the man lay in his bed at night, he told his wife what he had agreed. The woman got up, ran to the henhouse and clapped her hands, which made the cock begin to crow. At that moment there was still a hole in the barn. That was the blue barn in Olen.
171350: In the fifteenth century the dead Mr X was seen walking around at Kleidaal castle in Aartselaar. The man held his head in his hands and blood ran from the head.
171352: A girl who worked somewhere as a maid was ridden by the moon at night. The girl tried to reach the window but could not get to it. When people were ridden by the moon, they slept with their eyes open.
171363: In a house where there was always a lot of cursing, the two daughters were quarrelling. One daughter held the little bird and the other the cage. While they fought over the cage, they cursed terribly. When the daughters were in bed at ten o'clock that evening, there was a knock at the door. The mother opened it and saw a gentleman wearing a tailcoat and with horse's feet. The gentleman asked: "Where are the daughters?", to which the mother replied: "They are in bed." The gentleman ordered the mother to fetch her daughters. Only when the gentleman had come in did the mother realise that the devil himself stood before her. The daughters came up the cellar stairs and shivered at the sight of the devil. The gentleman silently turned around and left. The girls could no longer move, so their mother went to the parish priest in the night. The priest came and stayed praying by the daughters all night. The next morning they could move again, and the whole family had to go to church. There everyone had to confess and take communion to break the spell completely.
171378: A twenty-year-old man fell ill after a neighbour woman had given him a drink. The man did not recover and eventually died. When his mother went to confession with the priest of Itegem, she told the whole story. The priest replied: "If you had told me that, this would not have happened". A witch from the neighbourhood had caused that evil.
171383: Some boys and girls saw a woman walking who was suspected of being a witch. One of the boys made signs of the cross with his finger in the woman's footprints. Then the witch looked back.
171387: Will-o'-the-wisps were the souls of children who had not been baptised or who had been given away. You had to leave a will-o'-the-wisp alone, or else it came closer. By praying a great deal for the lights, they would disappear.
171448: A soldier who had joined the army voluntarily had to go and fetch bread for his sergeant one day. The soldier refused, at which the sergeant got angry and threatened him with prison. When the sergeant tried to go to the soldier, he began to jump and dance on the threshold until the soldier said: "Now it's over". Another time the soldier stopped the brass band by drawing a line on the ground with his foot.
171463: Many people could not get past the Brouwwei between Berendrecht and Lillo. A man who could not get past the bridge had been ridden by the mare.
171491: A man who liked to spend time in female company often scutched flax with the women. One day, however, the scutching board could not be found. A witch who lived in the woods had magicked the scutching board onto the roof. Another day she had put the cow cart on the roof.
171493: Because Bans V.Z. was bewitched, he went to the priest, who said: "I will help you, but then you must promise to do everything I tell you". The man had to go on a pilgrimage and pray a paternoster at every little chapel. Although there had never been any chapels on that road before, the place was suddenly full of little chapels. Young women were walking about who wanted to chase Bans away. In this way Bans was freed from the witchcraft.
171499: A witch owned a book and a doll. She stuck pins into the doll to torment a child that way.
171529: On a farm that a witch often visited, the cows sometimes stood dancing in the cowshed. The animals there were also very thin.
171541: A man who had lost a child fell ill. His wife fell ill too. The people went to Bornem, where they were shown the guilty one after swearing not to harm that person. But the evil had already gone too far, and the sick people died.
171555: In a farmer's wife's stable there were always wailing cats. The farmer's wife went to the friars, who said: "Someone will come after you, but you must not speak." Shortly afterwards the woman was indeed followed by a sorceress who tried to step on her right heel. But the woman did not speak and so was freed from the witchcraft.
171562: Between Sint-Job and Sint-Teunnes lived a woman whose clothes always lay in the house smeared with mud in the morning. When the seamstress asked her where she had been, she answered: "To Hoogstraten, to d'Hees". When that woman lay on her deathbed, she asked her farmhands and maids for help. But no one was allowed to help her, or else they would become a witch themselves. On the day her body was carried out for the funeral, her well burst into flames.
171596: Two young men walked three times in the footprints of a suspicious woman from Ginderbuiten. The woman looked back, so the men knew for sure that she was a witch.
171607: A man was always given cherries and pears by his employer, a woman. Because he did not trust it, he threw the fruit into the toilet. When the man's wife lay dying, he told his employer that he would not come to work that week. To that the woman said: "No, just come to work, for she will not die this week". And so it was. Once, after his employer had patted him on the shoulder, the man ended up in hospital. There he was tied down with chains. During the Second World War the man was killed in a bombing in Mortsel. That was the witch's doing.
171613: In Nijlen there were three farms close together. On three consecutive Sundays a witch set those farms on fire at the same time. When people tried to put out the fire, the water turned black.
171617: Every evening Jan P. saw the ghost of his dead wife appear. The woman had promised to go on pilgrimage to Scherpenheuvel, but she had never fulfilled that promise. One day Jan decided to go to Scherpenheuvel himself. After a few hundred metres Jan saw the ghost of his wife standing waiting for him. Jan asked his wife what she was doing there, but she did not answer. The ghost went with him all the way to Scherpenheuvel. After that pilgrimage Jan never saw his wife appear again.
171674: A man returning from Schoonbroek with his horse and cart met a woman who said: "You were home so late yesterday. It was almost midnight." The man knew that was true. He decided to test whether that woman was a witch and crossed her footprints. At that the woman stopped.
171697: In Willebroek lived a woman who claimed that her daughter had been bewitched by a black cat that had come in and sat meowing in the house. The mother went several times to a fortune-teller in Brussels to have the bewitchment removed.
171701: One night a man saw a large ball of fire flying up through the sky. In the end the ball of fire burst apart and a black man leapt out of it. The onlooker believed it was the devil.
171728: A woman who had led a sinful life came to haunt the churchyard after her death with the words: "That damned world, that damned world."
171741: At night a drunkard swung a stick at a cat sitting on a branch by the road. When he saw the cat again a little further on and wanted to hit it again, the animal said: "Go on, knock me off once more!"
171746: If you saw a suspicious woman, you had to cross her footprints. If the woman looked back, you knew she was a witch. During mass the priest saw all the witches with a beehive on their heads when he said "Dominus vobiscum". Witches always tried to strike people on the back. To make them powerless, you had to strike higher.
171770: A man suspected a woman of being a witch. One day he followed the woman and made a sign of the cross behind her back. When the man made a second sign of the cross, the witch stopped and looked back. Terrified, the man ran home, where he made a third sign of the cross. After that he knew for sure that the woman was a witch.
171810: On a farm the pig jumped onto the chairs in the house. The dog there was bewitched too. All the people and animals there wore a medal.
171830: A sorceress read books by candlelight. When people saw through the holes in the shutters that she was sticking a needle into a candle, they knew she was busy tormenting someone. She always had a dirty, worn-out cat on her lap.
171842: A church is said to have once sunk in Grobbendonk. If you lay down on the ground there at midnight, you could hear bells ringing.
171850: A strong woman could not work and kept saying at night: "There she is, there she is!" The people went to the friars at the Bremkapel in Putte. On the way they met the suspect in the morning. The tormented woman was eventually cured after all.
171865: A man set off at three in the morning because he had to fetch pigs from a farmer. When the man was halfway between Groot Rees and Kastel-dorp, a black cat suddenly jumped in front of his horse. The man tried to chase away the meowing cat, but could not. The animal kept following him. When the man rode home, the same thing happened again. The cat only disappeared when the man reached the spot where the animal had first appeared.
171882: Witches could change themselves into small animals and so creep into houses to spy on people. If such an animal was wounded, a little later the witch could be seen lying in the same place in her human form.
171904: A man coming back from Branst was pursued by a good hundred meowing cats. The man could not chase the cats away until he reached the little chapel.
171941: A woman heard her child crying and went upstairs. When she got upstairs, she found the child sleeping peacefully. The woman had barely got back downstairs when the crying started again. The neighbour woman was a witch.
171965: One morning on a farm three cows and four other animals were deathly ill. The farmer rode on horseback to Puurs to get help. On the way, however, his horse stopped. The animal could not go forward and collapsed. This was caused by the evil hand, which had also struck the animals on the farm.
171985: A woman had much misfortune because of a witch in her family. Her husband died and many animals did not survive either.
171988: People saw marbles lying in a small pit. When the marbles had disappeared the next morning, they believed the pit was bewitched.
172037: A farm in Ramsdonk was haunted. It sounded as if four men were at work with flails in the loft. When the farmer got up, there was nothing strange to be heard any more. In the end the priest came to bless the farm.
172043: A man who had already lost many pigs found one day that one of his pigs was standing dead against the wall. The priest came to read prayers over the pigsty with his book in his hand and said: "You need not be afraid any more. You can put ten in there at once". After that the pigs all thrived. It must have been the evil hand that had caused the misfortune.
172048: A man who had to deliver butter somewhere saw a cat sitting on the way. He kicked the cat off the road and went on. A little further on the man saw the cat sitting there again and kicked the animal once more. When he saw the cat for the third time, he did not kick, but heard the cat say: "You are lucky now that you did not kick, or else it would have been the end of you". That cat was a witch.
172054: A farmer whose cowshed had been struck by the evil hand went to the friars, for all the animals in the shed were dying and the vet could do nothing about it. Then a priest came to read prayers over the shed. After that there was no more misfortune there.
172060: A farmer from Gelendel who had to go and stay with his sister one evening was, to his great fright, pursued in the Halstraatje by a headless calf. The man told his story, after which his family went with a lantern to look at the haunted spot. There the people saw a calf digging in the ground with its head. It was an animal that had run away from a farm.
172088: On the Horst there walked a man who had stolen a boundary post. The man had gone to confession and been advised by the priest to put the boundary post back, but because the wood had been cleared, he no longer knew where the post had stood. So every night after twelve o'clock the man stood on the Drieschoor calling: "Where shall I leave it, where shall I leave it?" One day a drunkard came by, who answered: "Carry it back to where you got it". After that the man was never seen at that spot again.
172104: There was an inn at 't Stokt in Millegem. One evening around ten o'clock a boy came in, deathly pale with fear. The boy said he had seen a woman in a hooded cloak standing by a door. Because the boy believed the woman was eavesdropping, he went after her. But the woman walked faster and faster and jumped over a ditch. At a certain moment the woman turned into a calf. When the boy went to look at the spot the next day, he saw the hoofprints of a calf there.
172141: Every night a cat came into a house through the drain hole for the water. One day the cat was struck on the head. The next day an old woman from the neighbourhood wore a bandage around her head. She was the witch.
172168: A woman saw a man in his shirt sitting in a tree. The woman hurried home and told her husband what she had seen. The man went to the haunted spot and saw two woodpiles knocking against each other there, although there was no wind.
172179: A church is said to have once sunk in Pulderbos, between Lille and Poederlee. On Christmas night bells could still be heard ringing there.
172181: In Sint-Job there were two farms, one called 'De Vraag' (The Question) and the other 'Het Antwoord' (The Answer). The woman who lived in 'Het Antwoord' often heard knocking on the window. The people in the neighbourhood thought the knocking had to do with a ghost coming to remind the woman of some promise. One night the woman saw a glowing ghost standing by the wall.
172190: People said that will-o'-the-wisps were the souls of unbaptised children.
172197: Whenever the men were visiting the B. family, the cows began to dance around, because a witch lived with the B.s. The witch could not die until she had passed on her arts to Colette. Colette fell in love with Gust B., but he wanted nothing to do with her. Out of revenge Colette saw to it that Gust could not get home. At the V. family's, the horse could no longer walk after Colette had visited there. When the people had received a nail from a paschal candle from the priest, they were no longer troubled by the witch.
172227: If you drew a cross in chalk on the church door at midnight and went to look the next day, you could see that the cross had turned black.
172230: When there were many caterpillars on the cabbages, a witch walked slowly through the garden waving her arms. Then the caterpillars could be seen crawling away through the hedge towards the street.
172233: In the 'kaai' (?) a fiery coach drawn by two horses always appeared at night.
172246: A stable hand always slept above the horse stable. When one night the hand heard knocking at the door, he did not dare move. A little later he heard something come in and crawl up along the walls. Then the man was pounced on by something. He wanted to call out, but no sound came. The man had fallen victim to the mare. The man put his hand in his trouser pocket and felt the medal he kept there. Then the mare disappeared.
172249: A man needed a doctor because he had a throat infection. His eldest son went to the doctor and, against his better judgement, came back past the woods because that was the shortest way. The doctor had given him a bottle of medicine for his father. When he was in the middle of the woods, he heard laughter and saw a thick fog. Then a wind rose and he was seized by someone carrying branches. He could not wrench himself free and heard laughter the whole time. He was in the grip of the mare. When with great effort he had freed himself and ran off, he could still hear the ghost laughing. He arrived at his father's drenched in sweat.
172254: A man wanted to put to the test a woman who was said to be a witch. One evening he visited the supposed witch and pretended to have fallen asleep. So he could see how at midnight the witch lifted a tile, took something out and then left. The man followed the witch until she stopped and said: "Tell no one what you have seen, or I'll make you pay for it!" On the way home the man got lost, so that he did not get home until the next morning.
172268: In Antwerp a girl went dancing at the Alkazar. She said: "I want to dance, even if the devil has to come and fetch me." The devil came to fetch her and left a burnt trail. When the girl danced with the devil, the gentleman stamped through the wooden floor everywhere.
172285: A man went to get eggs somewhere, but he had nothing with him to put them in, so the woman said: "Here is a handkerchief. Just put them in there". When he got home, the man threw the handkerchief onto the butter churn. After that he could no longer make butter until the priest had come to read prayers over the churn.
172294: On a farm two maids always saw a toad when they were cutting grass. Once one of the maids cut off one of the toad's front legs with her sickle. When the maids came home, they saw that the farmer's wife was wearing a bandage around her arm.
172297: A mother who had just had a baby had been visited by a witch. A short time later the child died. It had developed a small spot on its back. The mother believed that visitor was responsible for her child's death.
172318: Some hunters had shot a small white rabbit using blessed shot they had been given by a midwife. On their way home, however, the hunters suffered greatly. They were beaten and flung back and forth until they were drenched in sweat. The next morning the witch had to send for the doctor to have the pellets removed from her body.
172321: A woman wore a little white lace cap with which she could open a locked door.
172335: In Mol there lived a beggar woman who had a bad name. When she was given potatoes somewhere, she threw them across the floor, after which misfortune came to the stable. Not a single calf could be kept alive. When the eggs had been counted and taken to the cellar, the number no longer matched afterwards. People went to the parish priest, who came with a book but walked past the house. After thirty metres he came back and went in through the back without saying anything. He tapped the farmer's wife on the shoulder, after which the misfortune was over.
172363: In Deurne there lived a witch who made her husband lose his way. She would send him off for a few days and then he could do nothing but obey.
172365: Will-o'-the-wisps were unbaptised little souls that were mostly encountered in the broek (marshy lowland). Just like the Jehovahs, will-o'-the-wisps always came back again after their death.
172390: A farmer's wife who sold goat meat was always visited by a neighbour who came to fetch young goats. The farmer's wife urged her daughter not to touch the woman when she came to pay. She was to have the money put on the table. One day the farmer's wife herself did let money be counted into her hand. After that she fell ill. People went to the friars of the Kluis on her behalf, after which the woman recovered.
172391: In Kasterlee there once stood a haunted tree. Its branches swayed back and forth even when there was no wind. Sometimes music or the rattling of chains could be heard too. When you came closer, there was nothing more to be seen or heard.
172420: A woman was ill for a long time after being visited by a pedlar woman who sold cakes and mastellen (round bread rolls) (1). The woman had been bewitched by that pedlar.
172429: A woman who was pregnant late in life felt so bad that she believed she was bewitched. In the end she was taken to the friars of Herentals.
172434: A young man went with his father to the farmers to buy cows. At a meadow the men saw a fat grey tomcat sitting on a post. The father said: "There's a cat over there and there are no houses here. Let's hope it's not a ghost. I'll knock the cat to the ground with my stick." When the man came closer, he changed his mind and left the animal alone. A little further on, however, the cat was sitting on a fence post again. This time the father did knock the animal to the ground with his stick. The next moment the cat was already back on the post and said: "Knock me off again!" But the man no longer dared.
172444: Near the Kruisberg in Oppuurs lived a widower with his son and daughter. A flax trader from Kalfort who often visited them found that the son and daughter were bewitched. They both lay ill in bed. The flax trader claimed that a woman who came every day to ask what time it was, was the witch. After that the woman never visited again. The children went on a pilgrimage to Kalfort with the flax trader. On the way there they saw all kinds of ghostly animals, but on the way back they were cured.
172453: When people went to visit their boyfriend or girlfriend, they were always accompanied by a cat. People who kicked at that cat afterwards got a pain in their leg.
172455: A witch could change herself into a cat. A farmer out with his horse and cart saw a cat constantly creeping through the spokes of the cart wheel and between the horse's legs. The cat was given a lashing with the whip. Afterwards that witch went about with two black eyes.
172465: Two men were fishing for eel. At one point one of the fishermen went a little further on to look. When he came back, his friend said: "You're lucky you weren't here just now. There was a witch thrashing about in the water." On the way the man was always pulled into the ditch by the witch. The other man, however, did not see the witch.
172474: A family was always visited by a rag-picker woman who was a witch. The witch bewitched an aunt of these people. The doctors could not help that woman, and so she died.
172482: When walking along the paved road, you could hear the bell in the loam bell pit in Zemst ringing.
172510: Four people who had gone to deliver butter saw a floating figure in a lane in Meerhout. Three of them ran away; only one man had the courage to stay where he was.
172533: Some people coming back from the torekeskermis (tower fair) in Schilde saw a mewing cat sitting on the road. One of the men kicked the animal a good ten metres. A little later the cat was sitting in front of them again. The man said a prayer he had learned from the priest, after which the cat sat still. When they were so far away that they normally could no longer have heard the cat, they still heard the mewing. With his special prayers that man could fix any people and animals to the spot if he wanted. He had learned all those prayers from a clergyman. For example, he said: "I let you stand as Jesus did with Pilate" to fix someone, and "I let you go, as Jesus did with Pilate" to release someone.
172540: On the Achterheide in 's Gravenhage stood a mill. The miller had already employed many farmhands. The farmhands were always attacked and murdered at night, so that the miller could no longer find anyone willing to work for him. One day a brave fellow applied. On his first evening the farmhand took a knife to his room and stayed awake. At midnight he saw the door open and a horse's leg appeared. The farmhand chopped off the leg and heard a scream. The next morning the miller's wife lay in her bed with one hand. The severed hand lay beside her.
172553: In Retie lived a man who consorted with the devil. One day that man had once again been thrown into prison. He had been tied up and the door had been locked. But the wizard said to the guard: "I'm buying the wine. Where shall we drink it?" After work the guard went to the café, where he saw the wizard already sitting.
172572: Between midnight and one o'clock the witches held gatherings, so that there were thirty or forty cats in Weelde. In Poppel there were even more, though, because there the witches could dance around the church.
172636: In a house in Ginderbroek the cups danced on the table. The occupants had the parish priest come to bless the house. The priest asked the people whether they had made a promise. After the people had the promised masses said for a dead relative, nothing strange happened in the house any more.
172672: In the French period soldiers often visited a farm. One day the people told the soldiers that a child of theirs was ill and that a woman came to visit every day. The soldiers took a little bird from under the roof and burned it in the fire. When the next day the visitor's children came to play at the farm, they were asked: "Where is your mother?" The children answered: "Oh, she has burned herself."
172684: A farmhand worked on a farm where a witch lived. Because a cat jumped at the farmhand every evening, the farmer advised him to strike the animal with a branch. When the farmhand came to the farm the next day, the farmer's wife lay in bed with a broken arm. The farmhand was dismissed.
172710: A poacher from Tessenderlo had shot a hare dead. Later the man found out that he had killed his own wife.
172721: A farmer and his wife went to live at the Schildershoeve. The first woman who came to them for milk was a witch. When the farmer's wife's first baby was nine weeks old, it began to cry every evening at sunset and had fits. An aunt went to Dendermonde for the baby, where a friar said: "You are too late, for the baby is dead."
172741: A midwife who lived in Heist-op-den-Berg always had someone accompany her when she had to go home at night. The companion walked behind the midwife. Beforehand she said to that person: "Whatever you see, you must say nothing." The companion saw large, terrible cats appear and sweated water and blood. That midwife was a witch, but she never did anyone harm.
172744: On Saturdays people in the village did not visit their boyfriend or girlfriend. On that day the cats went out on 'Merode' to eavesdrop on everyone. They then knew what the lovers had said to each other and went to discuss it with the witches.
172758: A girl of seventeen or eighteen often saw an old woman on her way to work. When the girl came home one evening, she saw the woman again and accidentally stepped on her umbrella. The woman often tried to get near children and gave them chocolate and sweets. When someone was bewitched, they had to go to the monastery of Tongerlo. The witch could be seen appearing in the shape of a dog or a cat. Those animals were sometimes seen sitting by a child's cradle.
172801: A boy who was coming back from Kapellen with his girlfriend said to the girl: "You go on ahead. If you meet anything, just throw a big white handkerchief at it". The boy had barely left when the girl saw a big black dog coming and threw the white handkerchief. When her boyfriend came back, the girl saw the pieces of the handkerchief sticking out between his teeth. The girl ran away and never saw the boy again.
172816: If you walked in a witch's footsteps in the evening, the witch would look back. In Zoersel lived a witch who was always out at night. In some places she threw sand. Afterwards the branches broke off the trees there.
172826: In Mechelen lived a woman who was said to be able to take the shape of an animal. When a disease had broken out in the stable of a nearby farm, the farmer found a large toad while cleaning his stable. He stabbed the animal with a dung fork. The next day the suspected woman lay wounded in bed. One day a black cat was given a thrashing. The next day the sorceress lay in bed beaten black and blue.
172829: A witch who wanted to get rid of her power had given a boy some coins. Shortly afterwards the boy fell ill. The parish priest came to read prayers over the bewitched boy, and the witch was never seen in the area again.
172831: A man coming back from Westerlo saw two or three howling cats sitting there that would not leave. The man jumped off his bicycle and kicked at the cats, but they would not be chased away. The man's dog did not go after the cats. A little further on the man fell off his bicycle, after which he had a lot of trouble with his arm.
172837: A farmer had to take a fourteen-year-old boy home. Between Massenhoven and Oelegem the boy kept shouting: "Hold me! Hold me, because it's coming over me again!" That boy was bewitched.
172846: A woman who had bought sweets put them all in the stove when she got home, because she did not trust the sweet seller. After that the woman suffered terribly. She never set foot in the sweet shop again.
172855:
A mother had a little daughter who was blind. When the mother was milking the cow in the evening, a toad came out of the pigsty. The mother said to her husband: "That is a witch, kill her!" On the second evening the father killed the toad.
The mother went to Scherpenheuvel with her daughter, who had then been blind for nine months. During the evening service the child could see, but when she went outside again she was blind once more. The next day the mother was visited by a woman who said: "Let's go to the woods, for there is a tree there that is good for the eyes." The mother cut down the tree and took out the inside. She mixed it with green soap and salt and put it on her daughter's eyes and wrists. Two weeks later the girl could see. The daughter had probably been struck by the kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft).
172864: A man who had gone to play cards had to pass a witch's house on his way home. Suddenly he saw a whole row of candles coming after him there. He was scared to death.
172930: A child playing by the dike was stroked on the head by a woman. After that the child began to cry and the mother did not know what to do. She took the child by tram to the friars of Mechelen. The clergymen predicted that the mother would not see the witch again. When the mother went outside, the witch was standing by the gate and left at once. After that she indeed never saw the witch again, and the child was good.
172974: A farmer was visited by a man peddling rat poison. The farmer did not want to buy anything because he had no rats. Shortly afterwards the farm was swarming with rats. There were even white ones among them. The peddler had put the rats there.
172979: A witch could turn herself into a black cat.
173018: A little boy always woke up crying at midnight. He would shiver terribly and have his eyes wide open. The child had been ridden by the mare. That could happen when nappies were left hanging outside after sunset.
173019: A man had said that he would come back after his death. When the man was dead, he did indeed appear to his brother. The chair the ghost had sat on was burnt. The ghost said that he was in hell.
173025: A family whose animals all died had often called in doctor V.D.W. Because the doctor could not help, the people went to the abbey of Tongerlo, where they were advised to move. After a while doctor V.D.W. no longer wanted to come and said: "Just make sure you don't let those women sit at the coffee table in the afternoon any more." When the people no longer let those women in, strangely enough they had no more misfortune.
173031: In the old days, when people saw lights in the air, they thought they were the souls of children who had died unbaptised. They called these lights 'stallichten' (will-o'-the-wisps).
173036: Some people coming back from work at midnight saw a woman sitting by the ditch on the heath. The woman wore a hooded cloak. When the men said "good evening", there was no answer. The men walked on quickly. When they looked back a little later, the woman had vanished.
173039: A woman who was seriously ill was tormented by a witch. The witch had a little cushion full of pins. When she had pulled the pins out of the cushion, the sick woman was cured.
173046: When a disease broke out among the animals in the stable, farmers usually blamed the misfortune on the kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft) or on sorcery. A farmer was convinced that his calves were bewitched, because when the cows gave birth they began to low in a strange and frightening way. The farmer panicked, dragged the calves out of his stable and beat them against the wall. That was the best way to drive the kwade hand out of the stable.
173062: Some people walking along the Emmelse steenweg suddenly saw three cats coming towards them. The people believed those cats were witches.
173129: A man coming back from the Kruisweg fair met a lady who led him through the canal and then said: "Have I gone far enough with you now?", to which the man answered "yes". Then the woman went on and vanished.
173157: A man walking home saw that a magpie kept flying along with him the whole time. The man believed the magpie was a witch.
173176: In Nijlen lived a woman who had made many children deathly ill. Once, when she was seen walking in the street, people noticed that she suddenly vanished.
173194: On a farm the cows were set loose at midnight, even when they had been tied with two chains. One night the farmer kept watch. The man was attacked by a black cat.
173229: In Hofstade lived two women suspected of being witches. One of them sold syrups for a cent. Anyone who bought something from that woman always got into trouble. A mother who had had her first child was visited by the witch, who stroked the little boy's head saying: "What a handsome little fellow you are." Afterwards the child got 'de oude man' (the old man, a wasting illness). People believed the witch was responsible. Because a priest could not remove such bewitchment, they took the child to the fathers of Diegem. The witch also often appeared in the shape of a cat.
173232: A man going to the barber met a goat on the way that had big eyes and horns a good metre long. After much urging the man told his story at the barber's. When he had to set off home again, he was given a little dog to accompany him.
173244: In Oevel a cat always came to sit by the open hearth. One day the animal was given a blow that broke its leg. The next day a woman was seen walking about with a broken arm.
173258: Some people from Oelegem went to play cards in a café on Sunday afternoon during benediction. Suddenly a large horse's foot was seen in the chimney. It was the devil, who appeared because those people had not been to mass.
173272: In Herenthout a baby had died through the kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft). The body of such a baby did not go stiff after death.
173293: 't Rinkven was haunted because a soldier had once been murdered there. A cook who had to go and cook there for her daughter's wedding heard a loud knocking at midnight that went on for a good hour. The people who lived there were already used to those noises.
173307: A man was talking with a friend, who said: "I can give you rats." The man did not take his friend's words seriously, but two days later there were more rats on his roof than tiles. Sometimes five or six rats at a time ran over a cow.
173354: A mother had fallen ill just before she was to give birth to another child. A neighbour woman kept her company. A friar walked past the house for nine days saying prayers. One of the mother's little daughters was given a relic. One day when the neighbour was sitting in the house again, a son of the pregnant woman put the relic under the threshold. At that the neighbour began to shout and rage. When the boy took the relic away, the neighbour flew out of the room without touching the stairs. That neighbour was never seen again.
173374: At Easter a drunkard was still sitting in the café at midnight. When the man went home, he saw lights on the way. Because of this the man quickly went back to Wilmarsdonk. People believed that such lights were the little souls of unbaptised children.
173392: A girl had been deceived by a musician who went around playing at fairs everywhere. When the musicians had gone to play in Aarschot one day, they had to walk back to Booischot. However, they did not reach their destination. In the morning they were even further from home than when they had set out.
173410: A woman always heard strange noises when she had to look after her sister's farm. She would hear the sound of a moped and a knocking on the wall. When the woman went to look, she found that a calf or a bull had got loose.
173442: A farm in Emblem was haunted. A brave man offered to spend a night in the farmhouse on condition that he was given a pan and batter to bake cakes. While the man was baking, a leg suddenly fell down the chimney. A little later a torso and a skull fell down too. The man threw all the limbs into a corner. The next moment a complete person stood in the corner. That ghost searched the room for a pot of money hidden there. The ghost counted the money and put a note beside each pile to show whom each share belonged to. Since then the farmhouse has not been haunted.
173474: A woman from Lier always came to fetch milk at a farm in Kessel. On the mantelpiece of the farm stood some old plates. Once the visitor said: "You ought to give me two of those plates," but the farmer's wife replied: "We really can't do that, those plates have been in the family for so long." A week later the visitor came for milk again. The moment she came in, the mantelpiece split in two and she said: "You'd have done better to give me two, because now they're broken anyway."
173495: A woman struck at a black cat with a stick. When the woman came to that place again the next day, a woman with a broken arm was standing there. That woman consorted with the devil and had appeared in the shape of a black cat.
173541: On a farm eight calves died within one month. The farmhand's mother always came to that farm to fetch milk. The farmhand was dismissed, so his mother came by one more time and then stayed away. The people had no more misfortune.
173543: A man is said to have come back three times after his death.
173554: A man was annoyed by a cat that always came and sat on his book. The man must have hurt the cat, for the next day a woman in the village went about wearing a bandage around her foot.
173555: In Kapellen lived a farmer whose wife was a witch. When one evening the witch left after saying: "Over hedge and stile, to Cologne into the wine cellar", the farmer flew after her. When he arrived, the farmer's face was covered in scratches. He had made a mistake when speaking the magic formula. He had said: "Through hedge and stile, to Cologne into the wine cellar".
173582: A man who had got lost on the heath kept shouting: Come here, because I cannot get away. I keep ending up in the same place. The mare is holding me here.
173590: A wizard who had been locked up threw his cap at the keyhole. Then the door opened.
173609: When the friars came to preach the mission in Hallaar, one friar said from the pulpit: "Whoever is sitting with their back to the altar may go outside." The people could not see who that was. The sexton quickly stuck an Easter nail under the church doors, so the witch could not get out. At three o'clock she was still in the church. She banged on the doors, after which the parish priest was fetched, and he let her go. Later that witch handed over her books to the new parish priest.
173614: In the marshland lived a man who often went hunting. The hunter wanted to go out at Christmas too, although his mother advised him against it. In the marshland the hunter saw a hare and shot at it twice. Although he was sure he had hit the hare, the animal was not wounded. The hare ran to the hunter and sat up on its hind legs. The hunter reloaded his gun and shot again, but the hare was again unharmed. Then the hunter ran away as fast as he could.
173636: A man coming back one evening from the fair in Oud-Turnhout kept seeing something like a cloud jumping in front of his feet. Because the cloud kept hanging in front of his feet, the man could not get into his house. So he decided to sleep in the cart shed. But things were not right there either, as there was creaking the whole time. The man then let himself drop through the trapdoor into the horse stable and spent the night there.
173642: A man who could no longer move lay in bed. He could not even move his eyelashes or speak. The woman who slept beside him at night in a folding bed suddenly heard a noise at one o'clock. A black cat jumped onto her head. The dog wanted to bite the cat, but could not because it was tied to the bed so it would not jump on the paralysed man. The woman got up and searched for the cat. Although the house was completely locked, the animal could not be found. When the woman went out with her dog the next day and met a neighbour, the neighbour said: "Keep a tight hold on your dog or he'll bite my legs!" So that neighbour was still afraid of the dog, probably because of the events of the night before.
173644: After her death the mother of B. in Vorst came to haunt. Many pregnant women went on pilgrimage on Friday evenings to the place where the woman haunted.
173685: Will-o'-the-wisps looked like lanterns that flickered in the evening and moved back and forth. They were unbaptised children who came back. A man at the Kindermouw saw a light fly against a tree and then go out. The man went to look and saw only the wing of a dead creature. Will-o'-the-wisps were luminous moths that could be seen near a fen. If felled trees were left lying for a long time, glow-worms also appeared there, which people mistook for will-o'-the-wisps.
173692: Will-o'-the-wisps were innocent children who had not been baptised.
173695: A woman felt the mare come up from her feet to her throat. She could not utter a word and felt as if she was being strangled.
173704: During the First World War there was a farm in the Plankstraat in Mechelen with a horse in the stable. If that horse started stamping at midnight, it was a sign that someone in the neighbourhood would die.
173709: In Kiewit a dead person came back in the shape of a little dog.
173712: On a farm that was troubled by the kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft), a cow fell ill one day. The next day the cow lay dead with its legs in the air. In the following weeks several more cows died in the same way.
173720: A seventeen-year-old boy went swimming with a friend. When the two came back in the dark at about ten in the evening, they met a woman who, laughing, hit one of the boys on the head with a book. When that boy had been in bed for about an hour, his head was pulled backwards and he sweated terribly. The next night exactly the same happened. After a few nights things did improve.
173725: A market gardener driving vegetables to Brussels found on the Brusselse Steenweg that his horse would not go forward. Suddenly the man saw a black cat that kept running around the horse's front legs. The man gave the cat a few lashes of the whip. Afterwards the sorceress had bruises caused by the whip.
173726: A boy went to visit his girlfriend one evening, but it seemed as if no one was home in that house. A little later a big black cat jumped in through the window. The next moment the boy's girlfriend appeared at the window. The boy knew his girlfriend was a witch and wanted nothing more to do with her.
173740: In a brewery where everything went bad, a cat roamed about that would not be chased away. One day a farmhand chopped a paw off the cat. The next day the brewer's wife lay in her bed; she had lost an arm.
173759: In an inn near the Dutch border five men sat cursing over cards. When one of the players bent down to pick up a dropped card, he saw that one of the players had a horse's foot.
173814: A small woman wearing a hooded cloak peddled darning needles, wool and home-baked waffles. During a funeral the peddler stood beside a woman and said that the children would not leave her alone. The peddler stayed beside that woman the whole time. She could not leave, because the children were standing in her footprints.
173819: When there was a kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft) in a stable somewhere, it often happened that the friar who came there was knocked over. The friar could then get up again by himself, because he knew which prayers to say.
173831: If you walked behind a witch in the snow and placed your foot crosswise on her footprint, the witch would stop. When this was once done to a woman, she turned around and said: "I am not a witch, but I can do a bit more than others, that much is true."
173862: The people of the Hessie used to be buried in the church of Mol. The bodies were taken by cart as far as the cross of Ezaart. Under the coffin lay little bundles of straw, which were left behind. Later ghostly figures were often seen at that spot. They were the dead coming back.
173882: A black cat came into a house through the water drain. The cat attacked the people and could also bewitch someone. When the people put a holy object in the water drain, the cat could no longer get in.
173906: A man went poaching in the dark in windy weather. Because he had no candles left, his wife said: "I still have two blessed candles, take those". The poacher saw a large, thin hare and shot at it, but he missed. He tried up to three times, but could not shoot the hare down. The man went off and got lost. He ended up at the Vraaghoeve between Sint-Job and Schilde, where he had to ask the way.
173909: The witte madam (white lady) sat on a bush in Lippelo. One day a man struck the white lady, after which she disappeared for good.
173921: A fearless man going home at night kicked at a black cat that was running at his feet. A little further on the man saw the same cat sitting on a tree stump. When the man reached the farm, the cat was standing on one leg on the gate. The cat had also turned into a large beast. When the man tried to walk to the door, the lock burst apart.
173956: A witch from Mol looked back whenever someone crossed her footprints.
173962: When people had slept in the barn in the afternoon, it seemed as if their minds no longer worked. They had then been ridden by the mare and knew nothing anymore. A woman always said: Don't cut your toenails in the evening, or you will be ridden by the mare. The mare was said to be a standstill in the blood.
173970: Hardly anyone dared to go near the Halebeek because the brandende scheper (burning shepherd) wandered there. That was the spirit of a dead man who had to come back to atone because he had moved a boundary post during his life.
173977: When the coachman had to go and fetch the baron of Balenwezel in Herentals, ghosts danced around the coach all the way through the woods. The next day the horses were deathly ill.
173998: A man who could work magic was able to make a farmer stand still while he was sowing.
174031: In Brecht lived a woman who could change herself into a hare. When the hare was once shot in the leg, it was discovered that this woman had a hole in her hand. The witch sent a man to his grave.
174049: On a farm the farmer found that a hare was coming to eat the cabbages. According to the farmer the hare was a witch. The farmer shot the witch dead in the shape of a hare.
174052: A woman from Oosterwijk (Houtvenne) who was about to leave for church saw a will-o'-the-wisp on the chimney. People thought the house was on fire. Will-o'-the-wisps were the souls of unbaptised children.
174060: In a house a child had fallen ill after a woman had come to borrow a white loaf. A witch doctor from Diest knew what had happened without being told. The bewitched child died in the end all the same.
174079: Near 't Heilige-Geestbos lived a man who read 'De Rode Ruiter' (The Red Rider). One night the man sensed that thieves were stealing from him and said to his wife: "Go and fetch the dung fork". The woman got up, but the dung fork already flew towards her by itself. The wizard gave the thieves a good beating with the dung fork. Then the thieves had to stay standing where they were.
174096: The witheren (Norbertine canons) sent for the shepherd to determine where the village boundaries lay. The shepherd put a schepper (scoop) under his cap and put Postel soil in his shoes. Then he swore by the schepper (both 'creator' and 'scoop') that he was standing on Postel ground. After his death the shepherd had to haunt as punishment in the form of a fire.
174101: In Zammel lived a witch master who one evening drew a circle on the ground and whistled on his fingers to summon all the witches of the region. Shortly afterwards white cats came running to the circle from everywhere. The witch master made the cats jump, dance and fight. Then he made a sign with his hand, at which all the cats disappeared.
174122: A man coming back from the shoemaker in Oosterlo one evening suddenly saw a white figure floating towards him along the road in a lane. The figure was a woman who floated past in silence.
174137: When the eldest son of a farming family on the Keten had died, the farmer's wife turned out to be too stingy to have masses said. One evening the ghost of the dead son was heard rattling the stable door. When people went to look, the ghost was already gone. One evening, when the farmer was sitting alone in the stable, the ghost of the dead son appeared without any door having been opened. The ghost said to the farmer: "Father, have the masses said for me that I need, for I can expect nothing from mother". After the farmer had secretly had thirty masses said, the ghost appeared no more.
174165: A man always saw a hare eating his clover. The man tried to shoot the hare, but failed. Only when he had put his bullets in holy water did he hit it. A little later, however, the man saw a black dog sitting there, which came to tease him. When the man had chased the dog away, a large white cat was sitting there.
174194: Will-o'-the-wisps were the little souls of unbaptised children who had been stillborn or had died immediately after their death. The lights were seen mostly in marshes and low-lying areas.
174201: A man going home in the evening had to walk across three tracks. The man could not get past a house where a witch lived.
174208: A farmer and his farmhand went home together. Through the open stable door they saw a cow with a strange look in its eyes. Further along two cows had been untied. When the two had tied the animals up again, they went inside. There they heard rumbling and noise. They went back to the stable and saw that two horses had been untied. A while later the farmer's son wanted to go to sleep, but found a large black dog lying on his bed. He chased the dog away, but it kept coming back, while the animals in the stable started making noise again. The farmhand quickly went to fetch the fathers. One of the clergymen came with blessed bread. After that the strange events stopped. People believed it was the work of a witch.
174217: A woman was once given savoy cabbages by a neighbour. Because everyone who ate that neighbour's food fell ill afterwards, the woman threw the cabbages away. The next day the neighbour came by and said: "You didn't eat the savoy cabbages." She knew the woman had thrown them away.
174234:
A witch who weighed a good hundred and twenty kilos was married to a man who weighed perhaps only fifty. That man had no say at all.
The witch could make little dolls on the mantelpiece dance without touching them.
174247: A man was at the market in Westerlo to buy a heifer. But there was also a witch at that market who always came to stand near the man. A man who had bought a heifer at the market had nothing but misfortune with the animal and had to go to the friars of Tongerlo.
174278: Two farmhands had agreed that whoever died first would come and tell the other what things were like in the hereafter. When one of the farmhands had died, his ghost appeared to his friend, who asked: "How is it there?" The ghost replied: "Everything is strictly counted; even the meadow gate we broke down together is counted".
174351: At the V.W. family's on the Beukenberg all the pigs died after a witch had come to look at them. A friar of Tongerlo told the people: "You must pray for nine days. You must pray the same amount every day." The people were also given two medals, one of which they had to put under the door and the other hang in the stable. They were not to let the witch in any more. When the witch later wanted to come and look at the pigs, the farmer said: "Well, if you want to go and look, that's up to you." The witch replied: "If it's too much for you to come and look with me, then I don't need to see your pigs!"
174355: In a mother's house a black cat sat in the child's cradle every day. The mother always threw something at the animal, and one day she knocked out one of the cat's eyes. Later the mother once sat opposite an unknown woman who was missing an eye. That woman pointed at her eye and said to the mother: "Look, you did that!"
174371: A boy who had been in the army for five years was afraid of nothing. One evening he was sitting with some friends in a café near the little bridge at the Vondel, a notorious haunted spot. Although his friends advised against it, the boy decided, as part of a bet, to go to the little bridge at about half past eleven. His friends agreed to come to meet him from different directions. When the boy reached the bridge, a black cat was sitting there. The boy said: "I'm not afraid of you" and knocked the cat into the water. A little further on a woman emerged from behind the railing of the bridge and said: "You didn't think that was me, did you?" The boy's friends ran away terrified.
174379: In Berlaar there used to be several men who could drive away rats. They would say: "You rats, you ugly beasts, you shall vanish from my house, barn, stable and everything that belongs to me." They then had to send the rats to a farm with more grain, or else they came back and brought the rats from that other farm with them.
174420: A man on his way to the market in the morning met a ghost, to his great fright. When the man began reading the Gospel, the ghost vanished five minutes later.
174431: A woman was sometimes ridden by the mare. She would then lie awake and scream. It seemed as if she was bewitched. She had a standstill of the blood.
174469: A man coming back from 't Stokt (Mol-Millegem) suddenly saw a white figure sitting in a tree. The man stood still in fear and watched the figure float down and vanish into the air above his head.
174478: A mother who had a beautiful baby was visited by a woman suspected of being a witch. The visitor had barely left when the child began to cry. The crying went on for several days. Then the child died.
174492: Will-o'-the-wisps were the souls of unbaptised children that floated over the marshes and meadows.
174494: On a farm where three horses died shortly after one another, people believed the kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft) was in the stable. The farmer went to a witch doctor, who began to read prayers over the animals. The witch doctor also asked the man whether he wanted to know who the witch was, but he did not. After that the misfortune in the stable was over.
174504: On a farm in Itegem a visitor often came and gave the pigs in the sty something to eat. When the pigs were seven months old, they weighed less than when the farmer had bought them. The visitor was suspected because she was also known as a witch in the village she came from. The farmer's wife said to her: "If you can do that, then you may bewitch me too." After that the farmer's wife had fits. She had a baby that cried day and night for nine months and then died.
174550: A farmer who was in the stable because a cow was about to calve was visited by a woman. The woman stroked the cow's head and said: "You are clever." The next day the cow had a swelling on her belly.
174564: In a house there was a daughter who was ill. Whenever a suspect woman came into that house, the daughter began to toss in her bed and the cows became restless too. When the people churned butter there, the cream sloshed back and forth in the churn.
174577: On the Tongsken in Walem the ghost of the last knight haunted the place for years.
174583: Whenever there was a fair somewhere, people had the custom of baking cakes. When some women were baking cakes, they heard a cat call out: "Baking cakes and no money". The women had indeed not yet paid for their flour and were very frightened. Not a quarter of an hour later the cat was there again and called out again: "Baking cakes and no money". When the cat appeared for the third time, the farmer hit the animal on the head with a hot frying pan. The next day a woman in the neighbourhood was walking around with a bandage around her jaw. That woman was a witch.
174597: A curate who was praying for a sick child said: "The person who is doing this will come in shortly." A little later the witch did indeed come in.
174635: On a farm in Varendonk a bull lay asleep on a henhouse at night. That must have been witchcraft.
174649: In Sint-Job there lived a woman who was suspected of being a witch. A man walked behind that woman when she came out of church and stepped in her footprints. As long as the man kept his foot on the footprint, the witch stood still.
174675: A woman who was ridden by the mare could not call out or move. For a moment she even thought she was dead.
174676: A child died the day after being touched by a suspect woman. In the past many children died because they were not properly fed.
174686: A man who was town crier for the town and the notary was coming home through the woods in the dark one evening after a sale, when he met a woman who asked: "X, are you going home?" The man answered "yes", to which the woman said: "As long as you're sure of that." After that the man lost his way, although he knew the road well. The man lay down and fell asleep. The next morning he woke up under a tree in which a little bird was singing. When the little bird flew away, the man followed it and so got back on the right road.
174693: Two men went on foot to fetch animals in Dendermonde. When the men came back, they saw a heavy woman in a white cloak floating around the animals. The woman's face could not be seen. Only in Weert did the floating woman disappear.
174698: One evening on the hoge Hei a woman saw a cat sitting on the handle of the well. She struck at the cat, but the animal did not move.
174703: A man who had hidden money somewhere came back to haunt after his death to point out the treasure. People found the money at a spot where they always heard knocking at night.
174749: Between eight and one o'clock a white ghost appeared in the Heksenstraatje, calling: "Where shall I leave it? Where shall I leave it?" One day a drunkard answered: "Take it back to the place where you got it!"
