174764: A farm was much troubled by a woman from the neighbourhood. Several times the cows there were found tied to the manger by their tails. The animals could not be touched or they began to low. If people went outside after putting the animals right again, the game started all over within five minutes. That was the kwade hand (the evil hand, witchcraft).
174802: In de Kievit the cats could be seen dancing around twelve o'clock. They would then sit on the horse of a farmer who lived nearby. A man had once seen a hare running in de Kievit. He had taken out his gun and tried to shoot three times, but strangely enough the gun did not work.
174808: Some men from Zoerle went to work in a factory in Achter-Olen. Near the monastery the men suddenly saw a burning wheel rolling along the road ahead of them. A little later the wheel changed into a white friar reading a book.
174812: Bells are said to have sunk in the Duivelskuil, and they began to ring on Christmas night.
174867: A girl fell ill after being given little shoes by a woman. The shoes were put in the stove, but they would not burn.
174874: On a farm in Geel-Bel a black cat always sat among the animals. One evening the farmer struck at the cat with a red-hot poker. The next day one of the neighbours wore a bandage around her arm. When asked how she had got her injury, she did not answer. She was a witch.
174890: A hunter on the heath shot at a hare three times, but he could not hit the animal.
174950: In a café on the Achterheide some men were playing cards. One of the players sat cursing because he had lost his money. A little later a stranger came into the café, said: "Here, I will give you money," and then vanished again. The stranger was the devil, because he had round feet.
174970: A man saw a witch come into his house through the door. Then the witch walked up the walls and across the ceiling and went back out through another door.
174979: On the main road in Ravels lived a farmer who one evening threw ashes at a black cat. The next day a woman from the neighbourhood was dead.
175029: In Geel a Jew had once been murdered and his body buried. People said that the Jew's ghost often wandered over the heath in the evening. This only came to an end when the murderer himself had died.
175039: A woman made a little hole that had copper coins in it. The harder the woman grabbed into the hole, the more coins she pulled out. She was a witch.
175061: People who had moved the boundary post of their field came back to haunt after their death. One then had to answer: "Put it back in the place where you got it!"
175066: An old woman suspected of being a witch was always around cats. She lived in a very small house. She was rarely seen by day, but at night she went out. Sometimes she was followed by ten or twenty roaming cats. At times she gave shelter to as many as fifty cats in her house. When the woman slept during the day, frightening meowing and screeching could be heard there. Nobody dared go near her house for fear of being bewitched. When the woman died one day, a hundred cats sat meowing on her corpse. The cats would tear apart anyone who tried to touch them. All those cats had to be shot.
175099: Some people coming back from Broechem were followed by a cat. The people chased the cat away, whereupon the animal ran to the house of an old woman from Broechem who had moved to Vremde. That woman was known to be a witch.
175106: A miller whose wife was a witch was working one night. The miller chopped a paw off an animal. When he came home, he found his wife lying in bed with one hand.
175129: At 't Withof near Hoogstraten people often saw lights at night. These were the little souls of unbaptised children buried there. If you prayed an Our Father, you no longer saw the lights.
175138: A man who went to play cards on Sundays always came home around seven o'clock. When the man was walking home one Sunday evening, he met a cat a hundred metres from his house and said: "Pussycat, where are you going?" The man could no longer find his house and ended up in Schelle.
175142: One evening people were playing cards in a café. When one of the men cursed, the other players said: "But lad, the devil will come any moment." A while later a man came in and sat down at the table with the players. One of the players noticed that the man had a horse's foot and asked his mother to fetch the parish priest. "One more time," said the devil to the farmhand, "and then you are mine." The priest came and prayed until the drops of sweat rolled down his face. "I am not leaving here," said the devil. The priest replied: "We shall see about that," and made the sign of the cross on the table. Then the devil had vanished. The farmhand slowly wasted away.
175152: A witch could turn herself into a cat. At the miller's, witches gathered at night in the shape of black cats.
175165: If you suspected a woman of being a witch, you could put it to the test. You had to cross the woman's footprints. If she then looked back, you knew she was a witch. A man tried this with two women and found that both women were witches.
175175: In Puurs, anyone who went in the evening to fetch water from a well near which a sorceress lived ran into trouble. When people walked past the sorceress's house with the water, the buckets tipped over or were knocked out of their hands.
175176: In Schoten a witch always sat by the tram track. Whenever the tram arrived, the witch had always vanished.
175188: Black cats were said to have danced around the old church of Merksem every night at twelve o'clock. Those were witches in the shape of cats.
175205: A man and a woman who had two children one day saw a witch come in. When the children were taken to church, their headscarves blew away in a gust of wind. Strangely, the scarves flew in the wrong direction. Because of this, people said that a witch had made the scarves fly away.
175252: In Hulshout a man had moved the boundary post of his land. After his death the man had to come back to haunt to put the post back.
175269: A man had left for work in the afternoon in perfect health. When he came home at night, he was shivering with fever and felt short of breath. After the man had been to the parish priest, he was cured.
175283: A baker had made a pact with the devil. When the baker was dying, he saw a small oil lamp with blessed oil burning before a statue of Mary. The devil appeared to him and said: "I have come for your soul." The devil had to go back to hell with a loud roar.
175286: A midwife who was out at two o'clock at night kicked at a meowing cat that kept getting under her feet. The woman was convinced the cat was a witch.
175307: Some men out together met three little nuns. A little further on the men met three big black cats. One of the men said: "I'll put an end to that" and chopped a paw off one of the cats. When that man came home, he found his wife lying in bed with one arm.
175328: In the old days people often told of those who had been ridden by the 'moon' or by the 'mare'. The moon had a strong influence on nature. For instance, there were people who were 'moonsick'. The moon also often plays an important role in werewolf stories. At full moon many shadows were seen, so people easily became frightened.
175333: A farmer who had moved a boundary post ended up in purgatory after his death. The farmer had to come back to haunt to put the post back in the right place. The farmer called out all the time: "Where shall I leave it? Where shall I leave it?" After a drunkard had answered: "Take it back to the place where you got it", the ghost had disappeared.
175334: A woman who sold cards, and of whom it was said that she carried the key of heaven on her back, used to give speculaas (spiced biscuits) to children. Still, many people distrusted the woman and for that reason forbade their children to accept the speculaas. It was believed that if they ate it, they would stop growing.
175351: One night a witch had walked through Hingene. The next morning, on every farm along the road, the cows had been tied to the manger by their tails.
175378: A fifty-two-year-old woman who had borne twelve children lay ill in bed all the time. Her husband had gone to the fathers of Dendermonde, who gave him a relic to put under the threshold. The relic had been there barely a day when the sick woman came downstairs to eat. She sat down at the table and said: "Now I will not eat until she has been here." A little later she said: "She is coming. She is stepping over the gutter now." The father looked out of the window and saw that it was true. In front of the door the witch fell to her knees and cried: "Jan, surely you don't think I would do that!" It was a midwife they had suspected before. But it was no use, for the woman died.
175389: On a farm in Minderhout the best animal in the stable died. People had seen a black cat walk over the cow. When a man was sent for, a witch knocked on the door and asked: "I heard a fine animal died here. May I have a piece of the meat?" The witch was thrown out at once.
175411: A boy coming back at night from the Herselt fair met a priest reading a book at the Kruisstraat. The boy said: "Hello", but the priest did not answer. Frightened, the boy ran home.
175443: A farmer who was tormented by a witch lost all his potatoes. After two weeks nothing but mush was left.
175452: A boy who was out walking with his girlfriend said on the way: "I have to go and relieve myself. If anything comes at you in the meantime, throw my handkerchief at the beast". When the girl saw something coming a little later, she threw the handkerchief and ran in fright to a nearby café, where she told what had happened to her. A little later the boy came into the café with the fibres of the handkerchief still between his teeth.
175467: A farmer from Geel-Bel who was mowing suddenly saw a black cat jump in front of his scythe. The farmer wanted to chase the cat away, but the animal kept jumping back and forth. In the end the farmer struck at the cat with his scythe and hit it. The cat disappeared, but suddenly the farmer saw an old woman standing in front of him with a wound on her foot. The woman raised her fist and then disappeared.
175475: In the evening white wisps could be seen floating over the fens. People called these wisps white women. They were the souls of maidens who had died young and had to keep wandering because they could not get into heaven.
175521: A father said to a farmer: "The first person you see tomorrow is the guilty one." The fathers were indeed proved right. The farmer sometimes bought a fine cow that gave a lot of milk. As soon as the animal stood in his stable, it gave no more milk. His pigs, which should have been fat after four or five months in their sty, still weighed the same. Witches were possessed and always wanted to harm someone.
175554: In the Boskant some people were baking cakes with flour that had not yet been paid for. When they began to eat, a cat came out of the drain hole for the water and cried: "Baking cakes, without money." The woman who was baking grew angry, flew at the cat and kicked the animal. The next morning one of the neighbours was limping.
175559: A farm in Zelare had been struck by the evil hand. They never managed to get a cow to calve there. Sometimes two animals were found in one halter, and often at night an animal stood in the loft. The neighbours were called over and saw a ghost in the pear tree. When people walked past, the ghost screamed. The people from the neighbourhood saw a cord just in front of the farm and followed it. While they did so, they kept hearing footsteps behind them. In the end they ended up in the middle of the field, where the cord led to a little hole in the ground smelling of sulphur. That was the way the earth spirit had come up. At the farm no picture frame could be hung, because in the evening it would fall to pieces. Yet the walls there were not hollow. The fallen pieces formed a name. Some people claimed that on that spot a sans-culotte had smashed a small statue of Mary.
175566: If one went to have prayers read over oneself by the fathers, the woman who had caused the harm would meanwhile go to the victim's house and try to get inside.
175588: In Picardië (a hamlet of Schilde) there was a large fen pool where night lights always appeared in the evening. The lights hopped over the water and danced back and forth. It must have been a ghost or something of the kind. The lights were also called 'stallichten' (will-o'-the-wisps).
175630: A boy crossed the footprints of a witch, who then looked back.
175652: People who were ridden by the mare suddenly saw a hedge or a gate in front of them blocking their way. They fell into something and tried to call out, but no sound came. Those people were asleep but could not wake up when they wanted to. When they did wake up, they sweated terribly.
175717: In a brewery where all the beer went bad, a cat one day fell into a boiling kettle. The next day the wife of the baker (brewer?) lay in bed with burns.
175766: A man named J. was sitting in a café with a sorcerer, who said: "I'll teach it to you too. I'll make the devil appear and then you just have to sign." The man didn't take those words seriously and said: "Yes, yes." A little later a visitor came into the café and said: "Who needs me here? Didn't J. call me?" Although the visitor did not know J., he walked straight up to him and began reading something aloud from a book. He wanted J. to sign something with a drop of blood from a wound. But J. refused, which made the visitor angry. The sorcerer made the wall of the inn swing open like a door, and a moment later the visitor had vanished.
175768: When her husband had died, Wiske had forgotten to put the house key in the coffin. Because of this, the man could no longer get into his house after his death.
175778: People who were ridden by the mare felt something sitting on their chest and had terrible dreams. If one could call out, one was immediately freed from the mare.
175790: A will-o'-the-wisp was the soul of a dead person who came to atone for some sin or other. A man with a post on his back, for instance, often came haunting, calling: "Where shall I put it?" That farmer had moved a boundary post during his life. One day a voice answered: "Where you took it from." After the ghost had put the post back, it was never seen again.
175801: When the animals in the stable were bewitched, the misfortune was blamed on a black cat that had been seen nearby. Most people were afraid of black cats.
175803: A farmhand working on a farm had seen the maid get up at night, rub herself with something and then say: "Take me over hedge and hedgerow to Sein in the wine cellar". As soon as the maid was gone, the farmhand also rubbed himself with the grease and said: "Take me through hedge and hedgerow". The farmhand arrived at his destination badly injured. Since he could not get home again, the maid said: "I'll take you home". She then made a large billy goat appear, which carried her and the farmhand home. The maid had warned him that on no account must he speak the name of God. When the goat suddenly leapt over the water, the farmhand cried: "By God, that's a big jump!" At that he fell down. He had to walk for three more days before he was home.
175837: A girl from Nijlen saw the ghost of her dead father appear every evening. The parish priest advised the girl to crawl on her knees to Scherpenheuvel. In every village the girl came to, the church bells began to ring. Seven days later the girl arrived in Scherpenheuvel.
175846: In a house with a newborn baby, a woman with a bad reputation came to visit to look at the boy. The next day the baby lay stiff in his bed. A few hours later he was dead. A year later another child was born in that house and again the woman came to visit. The sad events repeated themselves. The visitor was a wicked woman who bewitched the children.
175849: Witches had to claim a certain number of victims in a year. If they failed to do so, they themselves suffered from their witchcraft. One witch kept a hen with chicks so that she would not have to direct the evil at people.
175861: The will-o'-the-wisps that floated over the marshes were the little souls of unbaptised children. If you went towards a will-o'-the-wisp, the light rose upwards.
175864: In Gierle, a heksenmeester (witch doctor) used to come and read prayers when the kwade hand (evil hand) was in a stable. One day a farmer came to tell him that all his cows were sick. The heksenmeester went to the farm and began to pray. A week later the animals were cured.
175867: The two sons of the P. family were real rascals. The devil came to lie in a corner of the house, with his wings on the table. The open hearth was full of ash. When the boys had to come to church by order of parish priest B., they were so ashamed that they crept to the church through the woods.
175965: A man coming home one night saw a hen with chicks on the way. He took the hen and the chicks and shut the animals in the barn at his home. The next morning the man found a witch from Branst with her children in the barn.
175996: On the border of Lichtaart and Geel there is said to have once been a farm where a white horse often sat on its hind legs in front of the door. At the same time a rattling of chains, pots and pans was heard in the house. Two young men lay in wait with a gun and shot at the horse twice. But the animal stayed sitting calmly and the two shooters ran home in fear.
176002: A farmer was visited by a witch who stood by a cow and said: "What a fine udder. You'll get a lot of milk from that." There were days when the cow gave a lot of milk, but then on the following days the animal gave no milk at all.
176034: Three men had agreed that whoever died first would come after his death and tell the others what things were like in the hereafter. When one of the men had died, the others asked the ghost: "And how is it over there, lad?", to which the ghost replied: "Everything strictly counted and nothing forgiven".
176040: Bet V.D.K. had gone to look at the pigs on a farm. The next day a pig on that farm was dead.
176090: A man coming back from Antwerpen saw a white horse walking through the water. The horse walked along with him the whole time, even in places where there was no more water. That was no ordinary horse.
176094: Farmers who went to fetch beer at night sometimes met lights on the way, which settled on the horse's harness. Such lights were called stallichtjes (will-o'-the-wisps). They were innocent children.
176101: People who were ridden by the mare lay stiff as a board in their beds and seemed to be dreaming. If those people could call out, they were freed at once.
176102: In Retie there lived a witch who tripped off to church every day. If you placed your foot crosswise on her footprint, the witch looked back.
176121: On a farm with 2,500 chickens, so many died that only 400 were left. A neighbour wondered whether the chickens might be bewitched and advised the people to go to the fathers of Lier. The farmer's wife rode to Lier with her sister-in-law. When they reached the bridge, they saw a strange old woman standing there. When they arrived at the fathers, the same woman was standing there again. The women rang the bell and the fathers opened the door. The old woman tried to push in ahead, but the father said: "Stop, not you." The father gave the farmer's wife and her sister-in-law leaflets. He also read prayers over the women and advised them to put relics everywhere. When the two women came back out, the tyres of their bicycles were flat. But they had no more trouble with the chickens after that.
176129: A man from Kessel made a farmer stand still while he was sowing. A little later the wizard made the farmer carry on working as if nothing had happened.
176152: A wizard could open a locked door or a locked chest by throwing his cap against it.
176174: A miller who went milling at night always saw a hare dancing around the mill at night. The miller wanted to kill and eat the hare, so he took his gun with him. He hit the animal in the front and hind legs. When he went to pick up the hare, he found that it was his own wife lying there.
176177: In a house in Zammel lived three bachelors who always quarrelled and could curse like heathens. One day one of them cried: "I wish the devil would come in here!" No sooner had the words been spoken than a rumbling was heard in the attic. The next moment the devil stood before them. It was an ugly monster with goat's legs and horns. The three men went mad with fear and ran outside. One of them went straight to the parish priest, who had just finished high mass. The priest came to the house, followed by a large crowd. The priest sprinkled the house with holy water and then went inside, where he found the devil crouching. Then the men heard a tremendous thunderclap and the devil had vanished. When the priest left the house he was drenched in sweat and said to the three bachelors: "If you call the devil again, I will not come any more." But the three men had had enough and mended their ways.
176182: In a stable, deformed and weak animals were often born. Many of them died because of the kwade hand (evil hand). When a priest was fetched to read the kwade hand away, he advised the people to clear out and clean their stable completely. While the people were emptying the stable, they found a toad. That toad was the culprit.
176228: In Tielen there lived a witch master who one day invited all the bewitched people to come to the watermill. There he would unmask the witches. When all the people were there, the man lit a large fire, crossed his arms and waited. A few minutes later a black cat came walking up. The cat stood fearfully before the fire and then leapt into it, meowing. A little later several cats had already jumped into the fire, and the witch master said: "If someone in your family were a witch, would you still want me to unmask them? Even if it is your own mother?" The people hesitated for a moment, but still wanted the witches unmasked. Then two more cats jumped into the fire. The next day the mothers of two people who had been there lay in bed with severe burns.
176233: To determine the border between two villages in the Kempen, a shepherd was called in. The shepherd put a spade under his cap and earth from Postel in his shoes. Then the shepherd swore by the Creator that he was standing on Postel ground. As punishment, the shepherd had to haunt after his death in the form of a light.
176255: At the Wimpehoeve a group of white women used to be seen floating around every evening. People were very afraid of the apparitions. At midnight the apparitions went to sleep in the farmhouse.
176277: A man who always met a black cat on a bridge could not get home. He was advised to put his coat on inside out, and then he suddenly could find his bearings.
176279: Where the Rupel, the Nete and the Dijle flowed together, there stood a little water house on beams. Mieke Vloek pulled children who came too close to that house into the water. Nette, a boatman's wife from Rumst, claimed that a girl had once drowned herself at that spot. At night a plaintive woman's voice was often heard calling for help. People believed it was the ghost of the drowned girl.
176284: Some boatmen from Bikevliet who were moored in Antwerp heard a voice call: "Woe to you, Bikevliet, if I can get to Bikevliet, not one stone will be left touching another!" Terrified, the men ran to the boatmen of Eikevliet, one of whom said: "That is someone from the family who is damned. You must have as many masses said as there are grains in one kilo of corn. When you have done that, the dead man will receive his salvation from Our Lord". The boatmen began to count, but every time they were halfway, the grains were mixed up. It was an impossible task.
176298: A woman lying on her side felt a stone fall into her eye. She felt no pain, but could no longer see with that eye. A witch had caused the misfortune. The woman was advised to take revenge: she was to urinate in a pot, pour the urine into a bottle and give that bottle to the witch. The woman did not do it, and she did lose her eye.
176353: A man wanted to test whether a suspicious woman from his neighbourhood was a witch. He walked crosswise in her footprints, after which she looked back and said: "You damned wicked boy."
176363: In a house people were annoyed by a black cat that always came scratching at the door. One day they chopped off one of the cat's paws. The next day a woman suspected of being a sorceress lay in bed with only one arm.
176387: A day labourer was very good friends with his boss. One day the boss died of asthma. When the labourer went home in the evening, he heard the wheezing breath of his dead boss by the brook between the hamlets of Overbroek and Goorstraat. In this way the dead man wanted to make sure he was not forgotten.
176393: A magpie always came and sat in a tree. People had tried several times to shoot the bird, in vain. When they had the gun blessed by the priest, they were able to hit the magpie. The bird turned into a woman.
176413: At a small chapel between Herentals and Herenthout, people saw the devil appear at night.
176422: A man coming home one night through the heath and the woods was followed by a large white dog. When the man stamped on the ground, the dog stopped. Although the dog did nothing to him, the man was very afraid.
176493: A man just back from the army had been to a café. When the café had to close at eleven o'clock, the man walked home. Although he only had to cover two hundred metres, he did not reach his house until half past three. The mare had made him wander about all night.
176552: A man had to go to Hoge Miert, where a sixteen-year-old girl lived who had been struck by the evil hand. The son who lived there said that around eleven o'clock witches and cats could be seen flying around in the chimney.
176557: Some girls who went to the fair together were followed by a black cat. The same cat also turned up when one of the girls was preparing the cows' feed with her sister in the evening. They would boil potatoes or turnips with draff and meal. Around All Saints' Day the sister was so fed up with the game that she struck at the animal with a dung fork. The cat was only slightly hit and ran off. When the other girl went to fetch water the next morning, she saw a neighbour sitting outside by a heap of turnips with bandages around her head and hands.
176596: People who were ridden by the mare could not move a muscle and felt as if they were paralysed. It took quite a while before the mare went away.
176604: A girl heard from a man in the neighbourhood that there was a will-o'-the-wisp sitting on the hedge at Bouwel Schrans. Her mother would not let her go and look at it. Such lights were the wandering souls of unbaptised children who did not go to heaven but to limbo.
176613: A dangerous woman often came to visit a farm and could not be chased away. Every time she had been there, the cows lay with their legs in the air. The animals had been struck by the kwade hand (evil hand).
176617: A girl who was often ridden by the mare made the sign of the cross, after which the mare left her alone. Sometimes the girl wore a blessed object, because that also helped well.
176624: A farmer who had a lot of misfortune in his stable always saw a black cat among the animals. One day he threw a club at the cat, which then crept away meowing. The next day a woman from the neighbourhood lay in bed with a broken back.
176629: One morning a market gardener from Mechelen was driving to the Groenmarkt. On the Antwerpse steenweg the man saw a white cat constantly leaping at the horse's head, so that the animal could not move forward. The greengrocer grew angry and lashed at the cat's back with his whip, after which it ran away. When the gardener arrived at the Groenmarkt, people were crowded around a woman who had a blue welt right across her face.
176638: In a house where a woman had been visiting, the youngest child came home from school. The child drank from the visitor's glass, which was still on the table. Then the child ran outside crying, towards the visitor's farm. The family had to go and fetch the child back themselves.
176643: A miller who always saw a cat once chopped off one of the animal's paws. Afterwards the miller found that his wife had lost a hand.
176644: A pregnant woman always had to drink goat's milk. When the child was born, the mother got pains and could no longer move her right leg. One Sunday morning the mother saw the witch appear before her bed and cried: "Mother, mother, come and look, it's X!" The witch stood there with a child on her arm and a pair of scales in her hand. But the mother of the woman lying in childbed could not see the witch. The father was called, but he saw nothing either. The next day the woman's parents went to the sisters, who gave them holy water and a medal. The people were also advised not to leave laundry hanging outside or draw water before sunrise and after sunset. If the baby died, it would go straight to heaven. The mother was also given a thread that she must not lose. During a later pregnancy the mother had to go to the sisters again. She was given some water to drink with a thread in it. Shortly afterwards the child was born.
176662: A man from Vorselaar had to pass through a fire on his way home. Strangely enough, he was not burned at all.
176675: The devil appeared to a drunkard near the border of Essen who was cursing when his sick wife had received the last rites. The man quickly jumped onto the bed behind his wife, so the devil could not reach him. The parish priest came in and said: "Whoever has never done anything wrong may come in." No one came in. Then the priest had the windows opened so the devil could leave that way.
176684: Will-o'-the-wisps came back to the dike every year. They were the little souls of unbaptised children.
176686: A woman who could do magic led people astray. One day she asked a man: "Where are you going?" The man answered, but she said: "I don't believe you." After that the man could not make any headway.
176707: In Zandvliet lived a man from whom horses were always being stolen. After mass that man went and stood with his hand in the air. In this way he could make people stand still at will. The man could also make the wind turn.
176716: At the farm in the Boshoek the butter churn used to start pounding every night at the stroke of twelve. When people went to look, everything was normal again.
176734: A sixteen-year-old boy with an ailment in his foot could not be helped by the doctor. The boy's father went to the fathers of Tongerlo, who advised him to do penance for nine days and not to let any neighbour women in, since one of them was the guilty party. Nine days later the boy was completely cured.
176770: A witch from Nijlen made the plates dance on the cupboard at night.
176798: On a haunted farm there was always trouble with the horses at night. The animals tried to break loose. One day it was decided to keep watch over the horses at night. When they did, at midnight they saw a glowing cat walking over the stable roof. People said that this cat had caused the horses' frenzy. A witch who lived nearby had brought it about.
176826: On a farm where butter could not be made, people believed the kwade hand (evil hand) had something to do with it.
176850: A woman who had been given apples by someone did not trust it and gave the fruit to the cows. The next day the cows were dead.
176859: In a house knocking was always heard at night. People thought it was the ghost of a dead person. When a friend stayed in that house all night, oddly enough he did not hear the knocking.
176866: Some men who worked on a farm never got ham from the farmer and his wife. One morning, when the farmer and his wife had gone to early Mass, the men seized the chance to fry some ham for once. After frying it, the men poured the hot fat over the cat. When the farmer's wife left the church, she was completely burnt.
176885: A farmer whose cart had got stuck saw a man come out of a nearby house. That man laughed once and the next moment the horses moved on.
176892: In a house where a strange cat always came in, a child fell ill. One day they chopped off one of the cat's paws. The next day the cat appeared again without any injury.
176906: In the past people often did not dare pass the churchyard, because jokers hung about there dressed as ghosts in white sheets. A man on his way home was pestered by a cat that would not be chased off and kept jumping at his legs. The man kicked the cat a few times, sending it flying two or three metres. When he got home, the man said to a woman: "If that was the witch's cat, brace yourself for tomorrow!" The next day the witch came to that woman for a cup of coffee and said: "I can't tell anyone how I suffered last night. They kicked and beat my cat, and I had a lot of trouble with it all night."
176925: On the Ijzerenveld there was a shop that sold groceries and sewing supplies. One morning a woman with a child on her arm came into the shop to change a large coin for half-franc pieces. At that moment the shopkeeper's five-year-old son came in and the woman stroked his head. The woman left the coin lying there and went outside. The next night the five-year-old boy began to cry at midnight. The crying lasted about two hours, after which the boy went back to sleep. The next morning he did not remember what had happened in the night. Because the boy was inconsolable, it was decided to take him to the fathers. An aunt tried three times to reach the fathers' church with the boy, but each attempt failed. A bricklayer offered to go with the woman, and then she did reach her destination. The fathers read prayers over the boy and sprinkled him with holy water. The people were given a slip of paper with a prayer on it, which had to be put under the threshold. The boy recovered and the witch never came to the shop again.
176941: On a farm on the Lange Heuvel a cat always appeared in the stable at night. One night someone broke the cat's leg with a dung fork. The next day it was found that a neighbour had a broken arm.
176949: Two men coming back from the Boom fair went for a glass of beer at the Hooghuis in the evening. At half past nine one of the men went home alone. That man had drunk only one or two glasses of beer. At the stroke of midnight the man was at the Klein Bruggetje in Boom. Although that little bridge was only a hundred metres from the Hooghuis, the man had walked for two hours. Only on the bridge could he find his bearings again. On the steps of the Sint-Anna chapel two children with long loose hair sat playing marbles. Because the children did not look up and said nothing, the man was afraid and hurried home.
176973: In a house in the Begijnenstraat in Herentals a child was born weighing only 750 grams. In another street a baby had also been born prematurely. The mother of that child often came to visit in the Begijnenstraat. Her baby grew well, but the other people's did not. The baby in the Begijnenstraat fell ill and always cried at night from half past twelve to half past one. The family went to the Carmelite nuns and then to the fathers. "That doesn't exist, madam," said the fathers, but the family held firm. So the fathers advised them to make a novena. The child's mother saw the witch appear at night, but her husband saw nothing. In the end the fathers advised the people to burn everything the witch had touched. The family moved to the woods, where the child did better. But the witch came to visit there too. In the end both the witch's child and the child of the people who had lived in the Begijnenstraat died. Witches were forced to do evil.
176979: The dead Jan V.L. came tapping on the windows in Ranst every night. The gamekeepers went to investigate, but they saw nothing.
176985: A woman had many problems when she was possessed by the kwade hand (evil hand). Everything went wrong for her. The cows could not calve or the calves were stillborn. The harvest failed and no money could be kept.
177000: In Ranst lived a little child who could not yet read but could make mice. The people took the child to the parish priest, who wanted it to recite a prayer, but it could not do that yet. The priest said that the child should then take a good look at the prayer. After that the child could no longer make mice.
177009: A man was often ridden by the mare. He would then scream and be thrown out of bed. After that the mare was gone.
177011: A man always came to Putte peddling rat poison. One day the peddler said to a man who did not want to buy anything: "You don't have to buy, but I'll fill your house." A moment later the rats were running up the walls of that house.
177026: A notary who was suspected of being a freemason had many books in which he had written evil things. At the end of his life that man suffered greatly. His death struggle lasted eight days. When he had died, a black dog ran outside. People claimed it was the devil, who had guarded the notary so that no priest could come to his bedside.
177037: In Westerlo there lived a witch who could turn herself into a large cat. One day some men kicked a cat on its front legs. The next day the supposed witch had a broken arm.
177074: A farmer from Wezemaal had a farmhand who was suspected of witchcraft. Whenever the farmer had manured the field, the work was mysteriously undone and there was a dung heap there again.
177094: A man walked behind a woman who was suspected of being a witch. A moment later the witch stopped and looked back.
177098: A woman heard a man's footsteps. Then she felt the mare move from her feet to her head. It was a standstill of the blood, which left one unable to sit upright and unable to see anything.
177101: During the First World War a man was returning from a visit to the dean. The man had to pass a bakehouse where a woman haunted, who kept wanting to touch him.
177158: A woman from Wommelgem had seen a black cat. She did not dare harm the animal because she knew that black cats were witches. If you broke the leg of such a cat, the witch would have a broken leg the next day.
177175: A man from Oorderen who had been to Hoevenen met a kitten near the Platweg that jumped onto his shoulder. The man grabbed the kitten and threw it off the dike. A moment later, however, the animal was sitting on his shoulder again. Now the man no longer dared to harm the kitten. When he came to a place where there were houses, the cat ran off. It must have been a witch.
177228: It was said of a supposed witch that she owned a doll into which she stuck pins. The doll represented the witch's victim.
177244: On a farm three men were keeping watch over a cow that was about to calve. Suddenly the men saw a rooster crawl out of a bundle of straw at the back of the stable. The rooster jumped from one cow to another, crowed a few times and then crawled back into the straw. When one of the men went to look for the rooster, he could not find it anywhere.
177246: The Onze-Lieve-Vrouwekerk, like the Sint-Jozefskerk in Antwerp, is said to have been built on ox hides. The ground there was very damp, so the cellars were regularly flooded. A canal used to run there.
177252: A man coming back from work often saw a witch walking in a street, who could suddenly vanish.
177258: A farmer from Liezele was coming home alone one night. When the clock struck midnight, he was standing right in the middle of a crossroads, where he saw a coach approaching. In the coach sat two men dressed in black. Without speaking, the men gave the farmer a little book. From that book the farmer learned all sorts of things, and he did a great deal of evil. People said that the book came from two devils.
177282: In a house in Westrode the doors were always banging open and shut. A woman from the neighbourhood was causing this haunting. When the man grew afraid because his wife was about to give birth, he had a father come to bless the house with holy water.
177297: An old woman who had worked as a maid for a parish priest walked with a walking stick. A housewife who was ironing suddenly found the old woman standing behind her, although she had not heard her come. The next day the old woman came to call her, saying: "Come, the billy goat is loose." That was almost impossible, since the animal was tied with an iron band. The woman went to look and tied the goat up again. Five minutes later the old woman was there again, saying: "The goat is loose again, you didn't do it properly." Three times the goat was tied up again. The housewife no longer trusted the visitor and fetched a medal to hang above the door. When the old woman wanted to visit again the next day, she could not get in.
177305: A woman who had had a baby met a witch, who asked: "Why haven't you asked me yet to come and see your child?" When the little boy was a year old, he still weighed only three kilos. The child was also often ill. The mother took the boy to town, where prayers were read over him by a father who had as many as thirty-seven relics hanging in his room. During the reading, beads of sweat rolled down the father's face.
177310: One day in Zemst a dog was given a beating. The next day a woman was walking around the neighbourhood with a towel wrapped around her head.
177323: A farm suffered much misfortune. The animals died or were ill for a long time. This was the work of a sorceress who caught a toad, let it dry, and scattered the powdered toad over the grass the animals ate.
177346: A farmer's wife always felt as if she was being stabbed and was ill from the torment. Someone claimed that a certain witch was causing these torments by sticking pins and awls into a little doll.
177367: A woman had got lice through a witch's doing. After rubbing herself with petroleum, she was rid of the lice. In the evening, however, she was full of lice again. Wherever the woman walked in the house, a rattling could always be heard in the attic above that spot. Only when her father slept in her room was nothing heard. Only after a visit to the friars of Hasselt did the strange events end. The witch did not come by again after that.
177439: A priest came haunting at 't Schranske.
177484: A boy of eighteen or nineteen was ill for three months, probably because of a witch.
177492: In Lint twins were born. One of the children looked exactly like a monkey. The child was taken to the fathers, who attributed the misfortune to the kwade hand (evil hand).
177515: A man troubled by the kwade hand (evil hand) had much misfortune. His animals fell ill or died. In the end the man sold his farm and went to live elsewhere. There he had no more problems.
177540: A toad always came into a house through the water drain. One day someone chopped off one of the toad's legs. The next day it was found that a neighbour lay in bed because she had lost her leg.
177544: A farmer who had troubles saw the devil appear in the shape of a distinguished gentleman who nevertheless had animal feet. The farmer signed a contract in his own blood, in which he declared that he sold his soul in exchange for a stable full of healthy animals.
177555: One was not allowed to harm a cat at night. A man from Emblem once kicked a cat. When the man came home afterwards, he found that his wife had two broken legs.
177561: A sick farmer's wife was always visited by a witch. One day the farmer's wife's relatives went to spy on the witch in her house. They saw the witch sticking pins into a little doll. When they got home, they learned that the farmer's wife had suffered badly. Once they had the witch come and sat her by the hearth on a chair with a relic hidden underneath. The fire got hotter and hotter, but the witch could not get up because of the relic under her chair. They forced the witch to take out the doll she had in her pocket and throw it into the fire. After that the farmer's wife was cured.
177577: On a farm in the Bremstraat where there was a small child, an old neighbour woman came to fetch milk. She often touched the child. That farm suffered much misfortune; all the calves died, for example. In the end the people went to the fathers, who freed them from the evil.
177610: Magpies were witches and could therefore also speak. A farmer walking along the kattestraatje was spoken to by a magpie and ran away terrified. Owls were witches too, but the farmers did not dare to kill those animals.
177616: If people saw a black cat somewhere, they believed it was a witch.
177644: A farmer's son had been lying in wait in the snow for an hour, hoping to shoot a hare. At a certain moment a hare appeared, but the man could not shoot the animal because it was too far away from him. A little later six or seven hares appeared. One of the animals tapped the man on the shoulder with its paw and said: "Mister, there are quite a lot of us, eh!" The man went home and never went hare hunting again.
177663: A woman was suspected of being a witch. Whenever she had been in a house, everyone was full of lice.
177687: A mother was always visited by a sorceress who came to fetch milk. One day the woman's child fell ill. The doctor did not know what the problem was. Every time the sorceress was there, the child began to cry. One day the mother saw the sorceress stick a pin into her child. After that the sorceress never came to visit again.
177691: A man who was out with his dog in the evening saw a cat sitting by the road. To his great surprise the dog ran away from the cat. The man told his friends what had happened to him. When the friends wanted to come and look, however, they did not see the cat. As soon as the man was alone again, the cat said: "If you try to set that dog on me or try to hit me, you will find out what's what!" From then on the man never dared to come home so late again.
177696: A man who was accompanied by a black cat kicked at the animal but could not hit it.
177704: In Mechelen there lived two women suspected of being witches. These women occupied themselves with cats. When people saw a cat somewhere, they struck it, assuming it was a witch. Afterwards one of the witches happened to be walking around with bruises. People believed she had got those bruises when she was struck in the shape of a cat.
177705: In 's-Gravenwezel lived a girl who was always ill. The girl sometimes sat on hands and feet on a cord that had been stretched somewhere. In the evening she was sometimes so ill that she received the last rites, and the next morning she was cured. Witches always had to be able to harm someone, or else they fell ill themselves.
177741: A parish priest had bought a new bell for the church. He had taken the old bell out of the tower and put it in the porch. When the priest came into the church in the morning, the bell had flown away to a pit that was called the 'klokput' (bell pit). If you called out two or three times around the bell pit, you could hear the bell ringing.
177756: A man saw a burning figure with something white beside it. When the man tried to get closer, he could not reach it.
177782: A man walking home at night was annoyed by a pretty cat with a bushy tail that kept rubbing against his legs. The man kicked at the cat, but the animal kept following him. Finally the man bent down to the cat and asked: "Pussycat, where are you going?" A moment later a witch stood before him and said: "Jefke, what are you asking?"
177794: A wizard could make people stand still, so that they could not move a foot.
177804: If you placed your feet crosswise in a witch's footprints, the witch would look back.
177825: A man walking across the fields at night was approached by witches dressed in black who gave him a cup he had to drink from. When the man said: "In God's name", he was immediately freed. The priest took the cup away with him.
177882: A woman and her son saw a great fire appear on the road to the church. The other people could not see the fire.
177896: During the First World War a soldier heard a whistling that came from above. The man got up and walked into a street, but he was followed by the mare. He heard rustling everywhere under the doors and behind the shutters. The noise grew louder and louder. When the man told his story to the chaplain that evening, he was advised to be careful and not to walk around alone too much. The soldier was also given a medal, which he tied to the back of his bed. The next night the mare was there again. The soldier was woken by the noise that rang out at midnight. The man was so frightened that he flung his arms upwards. Then he saw that he was holding the chaplain's medal in his hands. The mare had run away from it.
177905: On a farm one night four horses were up on the haystack. The hay had to be thrown down through the window so the horses had a way to get back to the ground.
177933: A brother and sister went with the wheelbarrow to their grandparents to cut straw for the bed. When brother and sister came back, it was already dark. The brother pushed the wheelbarrow while his little sister sat on it. Suddenly the boy could no longer push the wheelbarrow and began to sweat terribly. He struck the wheel with his leather belt. A little later the wheel flew off. Because he could not fasten the wheel back on, he went to ask people in the neighbourhood for a pair of pincers. That way brother and sister finally got home after all.
177949: At the place where a witch lived, there was always haunting. When people passed there with a newborn child on the way to have it baptised, the witch always came to look. The child would then die.
177952: Some poachers had repeatedly tried in vain to shoot a rabbit. They chopped a half-franc coin into pieces and loaded the pieces into the gun. After that they did manage to shoot the rabbit. A woman from the village lay in bed with a wound on her buttock.
177956: A maidservant had a brother who had studied for the priesthood. Seminarians first learned evil and then good. That was how the maid had learned to work magic. While people were pulling carrots in the field, an apron was stolen from the house. "I'll see to it that the thief brings the apron back," said the maid, but nobody was allowed to watch. After noon the apron was back.
178000: In the Molenstraat lived a woman who was known to be a witch. One day someone had hung out the washing. Although there was no wind, the washing moved as if there were a storm. After a while everything was torn or tied in knots. That was the witch's doing.
178015: A man who was bewitched wandered about all night. Only in the morning could the man find his bearings, because by then the power of the witches had worn off.
178036: If a witch from Lier tapped you on the shoulder, you were bewitched.
178038: One evening in a house there was banging and rattling in the loft. People went to look but saw nothing. The next evening the noise started again. The occupant asked, "Who are you?", after which it was quiet for a while. Then the noise came back. A few days later the man sent for the priest, who sprinkled the house with holy water. After that the haunting stopped.
178061: A farm was haunted every night. Although the farmer had only two horses, the stable filled with horses at night. The animals were also drenched in sweat. In the end the farmer had to go to the monastery.
178067: The occupant of the oil mill in Lille went to the village to fetch a packet of tobacco. On the way the man was scratched twice by a cat, which he then kicked. A little later the cat appeared again and said: "Now kick me once more".
178078: A man from Oevel coming back at night from visiting his girlfriend, who lived in Olen, heard grunting. He looked round and saw that he was being pursued by a pig of two hundred kilos. When a cock crowed in Lille at half past two, the pig had vanished.
178080: A sorceress from Walem was caught at twelve o'clock on the Zennekant in Hombeek. The sorceress made all her children die, except one son. In church people all sat far away from that sorceress. Once, at the communion rail, the sorceress had bumped against a man's arm. After that the man never knew another healthy hour.
178084: In a stable in Ranst almost all the animals died and no more calves were born. A certain woman was suspected of having caused the harm and was kept out. A friar was sent for, who read prayers over the stable and gave the farmer a medal.
178120: A witch had placed a chest by her bed with a rooster or a crow in it. The rooster began to crow at a certain time.
178130: A man came into a dance hall in Averbode and said to a woman: "You are a witch." The woman replied: "How do you know? That's not true." The man said: "I'll show you. Go out the way you came in." Then the woman turned into a cat and went out through the water drain. Outside she shouted: "I'll get you yet!" When the man drove his cart over the bridge across the Demer, he fell into the water.
178164: In Begijnendijk a man kicked at a cat, causing the animal to lose an eye. Some time later the man met a girl who had only one eye and claimed she had lost her other eye in Begijnendijk.
178178: A wizard from Mol always rode his wheelbarrow into a gate. When the woman of the house scolded him, he said: "I do what I want. Just wait until tonight". The next night a great many grey cats came into the house through the water drain hole. The cats smashed everything. The next day the woman went to the police. In the evening two policemen came to keep watch. Around midnight they went up to the attic, where they saw five hundred grey hens. The woman went on a pilgrimage, but in vain. The next day the man of the house, who was a joiner, took his axe to bed with him. Around midnight the board was pulled off the drain hole again and a long grey cat appeared, which lay down on the feet of the joiner and his wife. The man struck out with his axe, but missed. The people went to the priest, who advised them to sprinkle the house with holy water using a palm branch. They did so and were freed from the torments.
178197: A chapel is said to have sunk in a pond. At Christmas bells could still be heard ringing there.
178201: On a farm in Buul people heard potatoes being thrown.
178206: Will-o'-the-wisps were the souls of unbaptised children.
178212: In 's Gravenwezel a woman had seen the ghost of her dead husband appear.
178218: A three-month-old girl had been struck by the evil hand. The mother and father went to the friars of Dendermonde, who advised them to do penance for nine days. After those nine days the child became healthy. A friar had offered to show the people who the culprit was, but they did not want that because they would then do that person harm.
178223: A bewitched boy was always pestered by a witch's cat when he sat on the toilet. The boy's father went to Averbode, where a father advised him to say a prayer for nine days. This freed the boy from the witchcraft.
178228: On a farm there was a cow that had just calved and so gave a lot of milk. The farm was often visited by two women who both had a bad name and who brought potato peelings for the cow. At some point the farmer found that the cow no longer gave a drop of milk. When the farmer could no longer get the horse into the stable, he went to the friars. As the farmer left, he saw one of the suspected visitors standing in the doorway. The woman asked, "Going for a walk?" and the farmer answered "yes". When the farmer came back from the friars, the woman was still standing there and a little later went inside. The farmer bought another cow. After that the woman's husband came to bring potato peelings, because she no longer dared to come herself. The farmer accepted the peelings but threw them on the dung heap. After that he got no more peelings.
178265: Between Grobbendonk and Put bells could be heard ringing at twelve o'clock on Christmas night. A church is said to have once stood there.
178278: On a farm in Klein-Scherpenheuvel lived a farmer of about thirty, who had three children. Almost every week a woman came to that farm peddling thread, ribbons and rosaries. One day some of the cows stopped giving milk. A while later the children fell ill. The farmer was advised to send for the parish priest. The clergyman said prayers while drops of sweat rolled down his face. Then he said: "She will come back. You must not say: 'Come in'. She will come back again after that and try all sorts of things to get in, but you must not touch anything, because then she will have power again. You must come and call me at once." The next day the peddler was there again, but she was not let in. A week later a rosary, a holy picture and a little ball of thread lay in front of the door. The people did not touch these objects and had the priest collect them right away. After that the situation on the farm gradually improved.
178300: Near St. Jozef a headless horse used to be seen walking around every evening and night. After a few years the horse disappeared. Since it had no head, it probably bled to death.
178303: On All Saints' Day people had the custom of putting candles on the gravestones. A man walking across the churchyard in the dark on All Saints' Day suddenly heard a little voice calling: "Give me back my little legs, give me back my little legs!" The man looked for the place the sound came from. He found something white beside the grave of a child who had fallen under a cart and whose legs had been crushed in the accident. The child had been taken to hospital, where the legs were amputated. Shortly afterwards the child had died. Because the ghost kept lamenting, the man asked: "But what are you looking for?", to which the voice answered: "I can't find my little legs, and so I may not go in". The man fetched two doll's legs and tied them to the ghost. After that the contented soul was silent for good.
178309: Along a remote lane near the Roefhoef a woman always sat haunting in the evening.
178329: A judge had a maidservant who was a witch. At night the judge's daughter sometimes cried: "Look, there she sits again, kicking all my carrots into the ground." The others could not see the witch, but they did see the carrots flying around. Another time the girl said: "Look, she's sitting in the garden behind the well!" The judge ran to the well with his axe, but could not see the witch.
178360: A woman saw a witch drop her walking stick right in front of her. The woman did not pick up the stick. When the woman was back home and took hold of something, she felt as if the object were being pulled out of her hands. The woman took a plate, which then fell to the floor. A little later the woman also dropped her iron. The woman was bewitched.
178387: New owners moved into a house where there had never been any trouble. The new occupants had to contend with the evil hand in the stables. All the animals fell ill and died. During milking, the pails were knocked out of people's hands or from between their legs.
178399: Late one evening a man went to the village to fetch a five-litre can of paraffin because his sister was in childbed. In the village the man saw the doctor and his wife sitting in a coach. The doctor said to the man: "You must stay here with my wife. I can't leave her here all alone in the dark." The man stayed with the doctor's wife until his feet got cold; it was summer and he wore no shoes. When the doctor came back at one o'clock, the man walked home along a long narrow road. Oddly, the road was covered with grain. Suddenly the man heard a droning near the ground, although nothing could be seen in the moonlight.
178414: In Olmen lived a man who owned a book of magic. The sorcerer could make five-franc coins and mice appear on the floor. He could also walk up the walls of the church. A man from Hasselt took the magic book away from him.
178420: At the churchyard strange things always happened between eleven and twelve. People said it was haunted behind the wall that ran around the churchyard.
178422: A woman on her bicycle met a witch. Then one of the bicycle's tyres burst. When the woman met the witch again in rainy weather, another tyre burst. At the factory the woman said that X had bewitched her bicycle.
178450: A woman was hacking at a toad in the bushes, while in a house a little further on an old woman lay dying. As soon as the woman had killed the toad, the old woman died too.
178456: In Geel there used to be a chapel where a ghost always wandered at midnight. The ghost briefly lifted the door latch and then slowly went away along the churchyard path as far as the barn of a farm. The next day the ghost was there again.
178459: In a house a dog always came and sat in the corner by the hearth in the evening. Since the dog turned out to belong to no one, people chased it outside, hitting it on the head with a stick. The next day a suspicious old woman was walking around the village with a bandage around her head. Everyone was afraid of that woman.
178460: A witch struck a little child on its legs. As a result the child's legs became very thin. Because the child could not be helped by the doctor or the friars, it eventually died.
178512: A girl went to Berendonk with her mother. When a woman in a hooded cloak was walking ahead of them, the girl said to her mother: "I'll put my feet in her footprints and then we'll see if she is a witch." The mother advised her daughter against it, but the girl persisted and said: "Oh, she won't bewitch us, because I made a sign of the cross with holy water just this morning." The girl did as she had said, whereupon the witch stopped and turned around.
178522: If you met a witch, you had to try to walk in her footprints to make her powerless. If she was a real witch, she would look back. A strange witch once lived in Morkhoven.
178533: A farmer always heard his cows rattling their chains when he lay in bed. Whenever the farmer got up, he always saw a black cat running away. After that he no longer heard the rattling.
178564: A woman had been murdered on a farm. The killers had eaten one buttock of the corpse. The next night everything in that farmhouse was turned upside down. Above the cooking pot in which the buttock had been prepared, a voice rang out: "Bones have lain in here. Bones have lain in here".
178570: Witches usually appeared in the shape of cats. Witches could be recognised by putting a clover leaf in one's missal at the Gospel of Saint John. If one prayed the Gospel of Saint John and then five Our Fathers and five Hail Marys, one could see the witches in church. The priest also saw the witches when he turned around during the 'Orate Fratres'. Usually, however, he closed his eyes, because he was not allowed to tell anyone who the witches were. If someone had been ill for a long time, people believed witchcraft was involved. They then prayed five Our Fathers and five Hail Marys. The woman who came in first would be the witch. If one saw a suspected witch walking ahead, one had to cross that person's footprints. If the person then looked back, one knew she was a witch. The witch could only move on once one had moved one's foot. If one put a holy object under one's door, the witch could not get past it.
178577: A man was courting a girl whose mother was a witch. One day the man took the girl home and told her he would not come anymore. On his way home a cat jumped onto the man's back and said something. While the cat was on his back, the man heard fair music the whole time. The girl's mother could only die after her magic power had been taken from her. After her death, moreover, she was completely black.
178605: If you wanted to know whether someone was a witch, you had to follow the suspected person. At the witch's tenth step you had to make a little cross with your foot. If the suspected woman was a witch, she would then look back.
178607: A witch could make mice run through the house. When the priest came to read prayers over the place, the mice disappeared.
178673: A man was coming back from Dessel together with a wizard. At the old mill the wizard said: "I'm going away for a moment, you go on ahead". A little later the wizard came back in the shape of a big dog.
178689: A girl who was coming back from the fair with her boyfriend had to carry Kleudde when her boyfriend had stayed behind for a moment to go to the toilet. The girl took off her apron and threw it over Kleudde's head. Kleudde tore the apron to pieces and ran away. When her boyfriend came to fetch the girl the following Sunday, she saw that he still had the silk threads of the apron between his teeth. The girl broke off the relationship at once.
178718: A man who lived in a clay house by the woods went to fetch buttermilk. Because the man had to go through a large wood for it, his wife said: "You don't need to fetch milk." The man went anyway, but in the wood all the trees fell down, as if devils were at work. It was his wife who had caused these strange events.
178727: In one house the children always fell ill after a certain peddler woman had visited. That peddler woman stuck pins and other things into the pillows.
178729: Because Eugenie was bewitched, the parish priest told her to walk around the house on three consecutive evenings and read the Gospel of Saint John. As the priest had predicted, the witch came by on the third day. The priest rid the witch of her arts.
178778: A witch doctor was called to a bewitched girl in the neighbourhood. The man shook his head and said: "You have come far too late. The child will die within two days!" By the second day the child was indeed dead.
178779: In a house there was a stone bench in the kitchen. Rats always sat on that bench; they came in through the drain hole for the water. While the woman of the house was peeling potatoes, the rats took the potatoes away. All the cows on the farm died. A neighbour woman had stroked a cow on the head, saying: "Oh, little beast, must you suffer so?..." The next day the cow was dead. A while later the horse also lay dead. Its eyes had been knocked out of its head. The pigs lay dead in the sty with a straw around their bodies. A man came to the farm who said prayers for hours and then said: "Now the one who did this will come by and offer something." The man also read prayers over mother and daughter, because otherwise the evil would pass to them, he claimed. The next Sunday the people went to early Mass, where they met the witch. She patted the farmer's wife on the shoulder and said: "You may come and fetch as much milk as you like."
178830: A rag-and-bone man drove with an empty cart and a black horse past the house of an unbeliever whose mother was a witch. The cart got stuck there, so that the man could not go on.
178855: A house was often visited by a woman who brought milk. One day the woman of the house was working in the garden. For that work she had taken off her wedding ring and put it under a stone beside a path. The visitor could not get past that stone and turned back. Then the visitor went inside, where she said to the woman's little daughter: "Oh, what a pretty child you are!" After that the child grew very thin. A man from Deurne came, who asked the mother to bare the child's right arm. The man made small signs of the cross on the arm and read prayers over the child. Then the girl had to go to sleep. The child slept all night and part of the next day, whereas before she had always cried at night. The girl was cured and gained weight again. When the witch was dying, a friar was sent for, because her death struggle dragged on and on. The friar asked: "Isn't there a little dog somewhere around here?" and he put a little dog in bed with the witch. The friar was barely outside before the witch was dead.
178863: At night the witte madam (white lady) came walking with a little light behind the hospice, where the Drabstraat is now.
178890: A man was afraid because he kept seeing the ghost of his dead wife appear. When the man said to the ghost: "If you are of the devil, then leave. If you are of God, then speak", the ghost pulled an ugly face and flew away in silence. After that the ghost never came back.
178902: A woman always came to a farm to fetch vegetables. Every time that woman had visited, the finest little goat on the farm went wild. The animal leapt up against the posts. The woman had given the goat something to eat. The woman also always brought something for the farmer's wife's daughter. At night the girl would then always wake up and clutch at her throat, because she felt as if she were being strangled. Because the doctors could not help, the farmer went with his daughter to the friars of the Oever. The clergymen attributed the harm to the witch and advised the people to pray a lot and make a novena. That did not help, however. Moreover, the farmer had great difficulty getting there because he always felt as if someone were pulling him back. The farmer then went with his daughter once more to the friars at the Stenenbrug, where he was given something blessed to put under the threshold. After that the girl was cured and the goat stayed calm too.
178962: A man had promised his soul to the devil in exchange for a new barn that had to be finished by the time the cock began to crow. The man's wife got up at night and clapped her hands, which made the cock begin to crow too early. At that moment there was still a hole in the barn. That hole could never be closed afterwards.
178968: Frans had promised to go on pilgrimage if his sick wife recovered. But the woman died and the man did not keep his promise. A few days after his wife's funeral the widower heard knocking on the front door. "Who is there?" asked Frans, but there was no answer. Frans then opened the back door and saw his dead wife standing there with a white sheet. Without looking at the man, the ghost said: "Sus, you still have to make three pilgrimages: one to Hakendover, one to Sint-Dimphna and one to Scherpenheuvel. Otherwise I will not stay in my coffin. Will you go on pilgrimage or not?" Trembling, Frans quickly nodded. The ghost then went back to the churchyard. The next day Frans was still lying on the floor. All his hair had turned grey. His wife did not come to haunt again, but Frans never fully recovered from the shocking experience.
178970: A man and a woman from Meerhout had only two cows. Because one of the cows was full of lice and also ill, they decided to sell it. The next day, however, the other cow was also full of lice. The friars gave them a relic to put under the threshold. Because of this, the woman who had bought the first cow could no longer come in. Two days later the other cow was cured.
178980: A man who was ridden by the mare at night could hardly breathe.
178983: A woman from Boechout had always said: "When I die, I will come knocking every night." When the woman was dead, a knocking was indeed heard, and a voice that said: "They count closely, but they forgive nothing."
179004: Some people who saw a witch coming by placed their feet crosswise on the witch's footprints. At that the witch turned back.
179015: At a baker's in Schriek there was a sick child. They went to a friar or a witch doctor, who said: "Watch out, that person is the witch. Keep the witch out!" The next time the witch wanted to come in, the baker sent her away. It was of no use, however, for the child died anyway. During the night the child died, the lid danced on the boiler and the stove would not burn.
179027: When Sus W. was coming back from visiting his girlfriend, he saw a light that came and sat on his shoulder. When he got home, Sus saw that the light had vanished. Such will-o'-the-wisps came from the churchyard. They were the souls of unbaptised children. When you saw such a light, you could say, for example: "Come here, I baptise you."
179037: An old woman often visited a house where there was a little daughter of about two. Every time that woman had been there, the child behaved like a newborn.
179049: In Nijlen there was a house called 'de Hand' (the Hand). The occupant of that house had beckoned to a will-o'-the-wisp, after which the light had come closer and struck against the door. Will-o'-the-wisps were the little souls of unbaptised children. A priest advised people, when baptising such a light, to say: "I baptise you and no other." Otherwise countless lights came flying.
179050: A black cat came to a farm every evening. One day someone struck the cat on its paw. The next day a woman from the neighbourhood was seen limping.
179094: A sorcerer from Retie visited his parents-in-law. He said to his mother-in-law, who was peeling potatoes: "Shall I make mice out of those?" He kicked the basket and the kitchen was full of mice. When he kicked again, the basket was full of potatoes again, but the mother-in-law could no longer peel the potatoes.
179109: A man who was visiting his neighbours in the evening kicked a kitten that was sitting there. He said: "Poor kitty, warm your bottom". The kitten answered.
179112: Four men were coming back from Antwerp with a cart. When on their way to Kessel they saw a farmer sowing, one of the men said: "Shall I make that farmer stand still? Just look back". The farmer stood looking with his hand in the air. The wizard said again: "Look back" and the farmer started sowing again.
179113: Some people went one evening to visit a farmer friend who was going to move to Antwerp. On their way home the people were surrounded by cats.
179123: Some boys playing in the street got a fright when a window pane in a nearby house shattered. A little later three more windows shattered. The police came. When it was completely dark the haunting stopped, but the next day it began again. The strange events went on for eight days, and the police kept watch day and night without catching a culprit.
179142: Will-o'-the-wisps were the little souls of innocent children who had not yet been baptised. You must not beckon to will-o'-the-wisps, for then they came closer.
179145: Between Londerzeel and Breendonk lived a man who cheated his boss by claiming many more hours than he had actually worked. When that man had been dead for some time, the boss was woken one night by a noise in the workshop. The ghost had to return until he had made up all the missed working hours.
179157: On a farm where the stable was bewitched, the dog would not go into the butter mill. In the past a butter mill was used to churn butter. That mill had a big wheel in which a dog was made to run. At night the cows stood three to one stall. That farm was under the influence of the evil hand.
179160: In the wood of Tongerlo lived an old woman who was suspected of being a witch. In the evening that woman often visited her sister-in-law. When the sister-in-law took the poker to poke the stove, and then stirred the pig feed with that poker, the witch said: "Tomorrow morning your pigs will lie dead." The next morning the two pigs were indeed dead. After that the witch was never again allowed into her sister-in-law's house.
179172: A black cat often sat by the mill of the Klamot, and people said it was a witch. They could tell by the animal's eyes.
179183: A man from Oosthoven was taking grain to the mill. But the man did not reach his destination and had to wade through water all night. Only the next morning did he arrive at the mill. He was bewitched.
179223: A man who always went to Grobbendonk in the evening saw, time after time, a cat sitting on a telephone pole. He claimed that the cat was a witch.
179244: In Dessel people saw many will-o'-the-wisps. Such lights were the little souls of unbaptised children who would not leave passers-by alone. You then had to say something to release the lights. But then countless lights came flying, and they only left their victim alone once they had all been baptised.
179249: A phantom hare came to the chapel of Klein Rees every day. Several men had already shot at the animal, but in vain. One day someone shot at the hare with blessed shot. This time it hit, and the hare died.
179255: A man had a daughter eight days old. She was a pretty child, but at night her little face looked like that of an old woman. The mother placed the child with a relative for a month. There the girl became healthy. When the parents took the child back home, it was dead in less than eight days. The child was bewitched.
179271: A farmer who had bad milk every day went to the friars of Bornem. An old woman who lived near Bornem was causing the misfortune.
179278: A man who was going to visit his girlfriend in Aarschot was jumped on by a werewolf on the way.
179295: On a haunted farm no butter could be made and the people had much misfortune. At night a whole army of soldiers could be heard marching across the loft.
179304: Will-o'-the-wisps were the little souls of unbaptised children. People who saw such a little soul said: "Will-o'-the-wisp, come here, I will baptise you." Then the light disappeared.
179347: During the First World War there were barracks in Urspeet housing sixty people. At night the lights were put out there and a cat could be heard miaowing. The cat jumped from one door to the other. People struck at the animal but could not hit it. One day a sick girl was taken away by a friar. Three days later the friar had managed to cure the girl.
179355: When a carter struck the water with his whip, lights appeared everywhere. They were the little souls of unbaptised children.
179364: Before the First World War a woman said: "Something is going to happen. I can see it in the sky, because the sun and the stars are fighting each other."
179365: A man went with some friends to take a cow to the market in Nijlen. When they had passed the Boekt in Gestel, they saw a woman in a cloak standing beside them. That woman knew that the man was from Beerzel and knew the names of several other people in Beerzel, although the man had never seen her there before. The woman also patted the man on the shoulder. The man wanted to strike with his medlar stick, but suddenly he could no longer find it. Several days later the man still had pain in his shoulder.
179406: The B. family on the Buiting raised calves. One day Sien V.S. had rubbed one of the animals on the head. The next day the calf was dead.
179409: On a farm where they could not make butter, the farmer's wife made three signs of the cross over the churn and also put some holy water in it. Because that did not help, the farmer went to the friars of Bornem. On the way the farmer lost his way through the doing of the evil hand. The friars told the farmer that he had to do penance for nine days. The advice was followed, and afterwards the butter was excellent.
179412: A man saw a dog drinking water by the brook. The man struck the animal with a stick, whereupon it broke in two and nevertheless went on drinking. The man ran away scared to death.
179452: A man who worked for a farmer in Opdorp was ploughing the field when suddenly he could no longer move forward. Behind him he heard something strange. He looked back and saw a meowing cat sitting on the plough. The man could not chase the cat away. It was a phantom animal.
179468: On the Schootse Heide neighing could be heard all the time because foals were flying through the air.
179470: A midwife who was married to a joiner had a son who was a tailor. One day the midwife was ironing when a woman with a bad reputation came to visit her. The two women stood talking outside the house while the neighbours secretly watched. The supposed sorceress fiddled the whole time with the strings of the midwife's apron.
